We make the source code and pretrained models available at https://github.com/NVlabs/stylegan2.

title: Alias-Free Generative Adversarial Networks
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: We observe that despite their hierarchical convolutional nature, the synthesis process of typical generative adversarial networks depends on absolute pixel coordinates in an unhealthy manner. This manifests itself as, e.g., detail appearing to be glued to image coordinates instead of the surfaces of depicted objects. We trace the root cause to careless signal processing that causes aliasing in the generator network. Interpreting all signals in the network as continuous, we derive generally applicable, small architectural changes that guarantee that unwanted information cannot leak into the hierarchical synthesis process. The resulting network matches the FID of StyleGAN2 but differs dramatically in its internal representations, and it is fully equivariant to translation and rotation even at subpixel scales. We validate our improvements by quantifying the robustness of the network to emergent properties like gluing, as well as the smoothness of the internal representations. Our results imply that incorporating principled signal processing ideas can significantly improve the quality and robustness of generative models.

title: Large Scale GAN Training for High Fidelity Natural Image Synthesis
abstract: Despite recent progress in generative image modeling, successfully generating high-resolution, diverse samples from complex datasets such as ImageNet has proven elusive. To this end, we train Generative Adversarial Networks at the largest scale yet attempted, and study the instabilities specific to such scale. We find that applying orthogonal regularization to the generator renders it amenable to a simple ''truncation trick,'' allowing fine control over the trade-off between sample fidelity and variety by reducing the variance of the Generator's input. Our modifications lead to models which set the new state of the art in class-conditional image synthesis. When trained on ImageNet at 128x128 resolution, our models (BigGANs) achieve an Inception Score (IS) of 166.3 and Frechet Inception Distance (FID) of 9.6, improving over the previous best IS of 52.52 and FID of 18.65.

title: Improved Training of Wasserstein GANs
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are powerful generative models, but suffer from training instability. The recently proposed Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) makes progress toward stable training of GANs, but sometimes can still generate only low-quality samples or fail to converge. We find that these problems are often due to the use of weight clipping in WGAN to enforce a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, which can lead to undesired behavior. We propose an alternative to clipping weights: penalize the norm of gradient of the critic with respect to its input. Our proposed method performs better than standard WGAN and enables stable training of a wide variety of GAN architectures with almost no hyperparameter tuning, including 101-layer ResNets and discrete autoencoders. We achieve high-quality generations on CIFAR-10 and LSUN bedrooms, and our method improves the state of the art on the ImageNet 256x256 generation task.

title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation using Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks
venue: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
abstract: Image-to-image translation is a class of vision and graphics problems where the goal is to learn the mapping between an input image and an output image using a training set of aligned image pairs. However, for many tasks, paired training data will not be available. We present an approach for learning to translate an image from a source domain X to a target domain Y in the absence of paired examples. Our goal is to learn a mapping G: X -> Y such that the distribution of images from G(X) is indistinguishable from the distribution Y using an adversarial loss. Because this mapping is highly under-constrained, we couple it with an inverse mapping F: Y -> X and introduce a cycle consistency loss to enforce F(G(X)) ≈ X (and vice versa). Qualitative results are presented on several tasks where paired training data does not exist, including collection style transfer, object transfiguration, season transfer, photo enhancement, etc. Quantitative comparisons against several prior methods demonstrate the superiority of our approach.

title: Image-to-Image Translation with Conditional Adversarial Networks
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: We investigate conditional adversarial networks as a general-purpose solution to image-to-image translation problems. These networks not only learn the mapping from input image to output image, but also learn a loss function to train this mapping. This makes it possible to apply the same generic approach to problems that traditionally would require very different loss formulations. We demonstrate that this approach is effective at synthesizing photos from label maps, reconstructing objects from edge maps, and colorizing images, among other tasks. Indeed, since the release of the pix2pix software associated with this paper, a large community of users has applied it to their own image-to-image translation tasks, which were never before attempted. As a community, we have still barely begun to explore the capabilities of conditional adversarial networks for image synthesis.

title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
abstract: Natural language processing tasks, such as question answering, machine translation, reading comprehension, and summarization, are typically approached with supervised learning on task-specific datasets. We demonstrate that language models begin to learn these tasks without any explicit supervision when trained on a new dataset of millions of webpages called WebText. When conditioned on a document plus questions, the answers generated by the language model achieve 55 F1 on the CoQA dataset - matching or exceeding the performance of 3 out of 4 baseline systems without using the 127,000+ training examples. The capacity of the language model is essential to the success of zero-shot task transfer and increasing it improves performance in a log-linear fashion across tasks. Our largest model, GPT-2, is a 1.5B parameter Transformer that achieves state of the art results on 7 out of 8 tested language modeling datasets in a zero-shot setting but still underfits WebText. Samples from the model reflect these improvements and contain coherent paragraphs of text. These findings suggest a promising path towards building language processing systems which learn to perform tasks from their naturally occurring demonstrations.

title: Neural Discrete Representation Learning
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Learning useful representations without supervision remains a key challenge in machine learning. In this paper, we propose a simple yet powerful generative model that learns such discrete representations. Our model, the Vector Quantised-Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE), differs from VAEs in two key ways: the encoder network outputs discrete, rather than continuous, codes; and the prior is learnt rather than static. Using the VQ-VAE, we demonstrate that we can generate diverse high-quality samples from a wide range of domains, including speech, images, and raw audio waveforms. We further show that we can learn a language model on top of the discrete latent codes, which can be used to generate coherent text and perform tasks like machine translation.

title: Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: Designed to learn long-range interactions on sequential data, transformers continue to show state-of-the-art results on a wide variety of tasks. In contrast to CNNs, they contain no inductive bias that prioritizes local interactions. This makes them expressive, but also computationally infeasible for training on long sequences, such as high-resolution images. We demonstrate how a combination of CNNs and transformers can be combined to efficiently process image-like data at high resolution. We show that the CNN inductive bias is crucial for learning effective representations, while the transformer enables global communication. Our approach, which we call VQ-GAN, uses a CNN to learn a discrete codebook of representations, and then uses a transformer to model the long-range interactions between these codes. We demonstrate that VQ-GAN can generate high-resolution images that are competitive with the state of the art, while being significantly more efficient than previous approaches.

title: Zero-Shot Text-to-Image Generation
abstract: Text-to-image generation has traditionally focused on finding better modeling assumptions for training on a fixed dataset. These assumptions can be complex, rely on auxiliary information (e.g., object detection), or rely on specific training protocols (e.g., alternating optimization). In this work, we show that a simple approach to zero-shot text-to-image generation can achieve competitive results with prior work. We use a transformer-based architecture that autoregressively models the joint distribution over text and image tokens. Our approach does not require any auxiliary information or complex training protocols, and can generate images from text descriptions in a zero-shot manner. We demonstrate that our approach can generate diverse, high-quality images from a wide variety of text descriptions, and that it can be used for tasks like text-guided image manipulation and image captioning.

title: Generative Pretraining from Pixels
abstract: Inspired by the success of autoregressive generative models in NLP, we consider whether similar models can also perform well on image generation. We train a sequence Transformer to autoregressively predict pixels, without incorporating knowledge of the 2D input structure. On a suite of image generation benchmarks, our model achieves competitive results with prior work, and is able to generate high-quality samples. We also show that the model learns useful representations that can be used for downstream tasks like image classification and object detection. Our results suggest that the inductive biases inherent in CNNs may not be necessary for strong performance on image tasks, and that autoregressive models can be a viable alternative.

title: Scaling Autoregressive Models for Content-Rich Text-to-Image Generation
abstract: We present Parti, an autoregressive generative model that achieves high-fidelity photorealistic image generation from text descriptions. Parti scales the autoregressive approach to an unprecedented 20B parameters, and uses a vocabulary of image tokens from a learned discrete codebook. We introduce several improvements to the training and sampling process that enable this scale, including a new captioning system that produces more descriptive captions, and a variational autoencoder that compresses images to a smaller spatial resolution while maintaining high quality. We evaluate Parti on the challenging MS-COCO benchmark and achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot FID score of 7.23, surpassing prior autoregressive models and diffusion models. We also demonstrate that Parti can generate images with rich details and complex compositions, and that it can be used for tasks like image editing and style transfer.

title: Video Diffusion Models
venue: ICLR Workshop on Deep Generative Models for Highly Structured Data
abstract: We present a new class of generative models for video generation that extends the diffusion probabilistic model framework to video data. Our approach, called Video Diffusion Models, uses a 3D U-Net architecture to jointly model spatial and temporal dependencies in video data. We introduce a new conditioning mechanism that allows the model to generate videos conditioned on a variety of inputs, including text descriptions, images, and other videos. We demonstrate that Video Diffusion Models can generate high-quality, coherent videos that are several minutes long, and that they can be used for a variety of tasks, including text-to-video generation, video prediction, and video interpolation. We also show that Video Diffusion Models can be used for video editing tasks like inpainting and super-resolution.

title: Make-A-Video: Text-to-Video Generation without Text-Video Data
abstract: We present Make-A-Video, a new approach to text-to-video generation that does not require any text-video paired data for training. Our method builds on recent advances in text-to-image generation, and extends them to the video domain by introducing a new spatiotemporal architecture that can generate videos from text descriptions. We train our model on a large dataset of images and their captions, and show that it can generalize to video generation without ever seeing text-video pairs during training. Our model can generate high-quality videos that are several seconds long, and can be used for a variety of tasks, including text-to-video generation, video prediction, and video editing. We also show that our model can generate videos with complex scenes and multiple objects, and that it can be used to generate videos in a variety of styles.

title: Imagen Video: High Definition Video Generation with Diffusion Models
abstract: We present Imagen Video, a text-conditional video generation system based on a cascade of video diffusion models. Imagen Video is capable of generating high definition videos with a resolution of 1280x768 at 24 frames per second, and can generate videos that are up to 5.3 seconds long. The system uses a frozen text encoder to encode text descriptions, and a series of diffusion models to generate videos at increasing resolutions. We introduce several key contributions, including a new architecture for spatial and temporal video super-resolution, a new technique for generating temporally coherent videos, and a new method for text conditioning that improves the quality and relevance of generated videos. We evaluate Imagen Video on a variety of benchmarks and show that it outperforms prior work in terms of both sample quality and text-video alignment.

title: Video Generation Models as World Simulators
abstract: We explore large-scale training of generative models on video data. Specifically, we train Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) jointly on videos and images of variable durations, resolutions and aspect ratios. We leverage a transformer architecture that operates on spacetime patches of video and image latent codes. Our largest model, Sora, is capable of generating high-fidelity videos up to one minute long. Our results suggest that scaling video generation models is a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world. Sora can generate videos with complex scenes, multiple characters, and realistic physics, and can be conditioned on text descriptions, images, or other videos. We also show that Sora can be used for video editing tasks like extending videos, filling in missing frames, and connecting two different videos.

title: Latte: Latent Diffusion Transformer for Video Generation
abstract: We present Latte, a latent diffusion transformer for video generation. Latte uses a transformer architecture to model the diffusion process in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder, which enables efficient high-resolution video generation. We investigate various design choices for the transformer architecture, including the placement of temporal and spatial attention, the use of positional embeddings, and the conditioning mechanism. We find that a simple design with temporal attention followed by spatial attention works well, and that using absolute positional embeddings is sufficient for good performance. We evaluate Latte on several video generation benchmarks and show that it achieves competitive results with prior work. We also show that Latte can be used for text-to-video generation by conditioning on text embeddings from a pretrained language model.

title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
abstract: We present a method that achieves state-of-the-art results for synthesizing novel views of complex scenes by optimizing an underlying continuous volumetric scene function using a sparse set of input views. Our algorithm represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network, whose input is a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (theta, phi)) and whose output is the volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location. We synthesize views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and use classic volume rendering techniques to project the output colors and densities into an image. Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize our representation is a set of images with known camera poses. We describe how to effectively optimize neural radiance fields to render photorealistic novel views of scenes with complicated geometry and appearance, and demonstrate results that outperform prior work on neural rendering and view synthesis.

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering
abstract: Radiance Field methods have recently revolutionized novel-view synthesis of scenes captured with multiple photos or videos. However, achieving high visual quality still requires neural networks that are costly to train and render, while recent faster methods inevitably trade off speed for quality. For unbounded and complete scenes (rather than isolated objects) and 1080p resolution rendering, no current method can achieve real-time display rates. We introduce three key elements that allow us to achieve state-of-the-art visual quality while maintaining competitive training times and importantly a high rendering speed. We start from 3D Gaussians that are optimized to represent a scene with a point-based representation. We combine this with an interleaved optimization/density control of the 3D Gaussians, achieving good visual quality. We also develop a fast, visibility-aware rendering algorithm that supports anisotropic splatting and accelerates training. Our system achieves real-time rendering on several datasets, while maintaining high visual quality.

title: DreamFusion: Text-to-3D using 2D Diffusion
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in text-to-image synthesis have been driven by diffusion models trained on billions of image-text pairs. Adapting this approach to text-to-3D synthesis would require large-scale datasets of 3D models and their corresponding text descriptions, which do not exist. We present DreamFusion, an approach to generate 3D assets from text descriptions using a pretrained 2D text-to-image diffusion model. Our key insight is that a 2D diffusion model can be used as a prior for optimizing a 3D representation, by using a novel loss function that we call Score Distillation Sampling (SDS). SDS uses the diffusion model to provide gradients that guide the optimization of a 3D representation (in our case, a NeRF) to match the text description. We show that DreamFusion can generate high-quality 3D assets from a wide variety of text descriptions, without any 3D training data. We also show that the generated 3D assets can be rendered from arbitrary viewpoints and used in downstream applications.

title: Magic3D: High-Resolution Text-to-3D Content Creation
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: DreamFusion has recently demonstrated the feasibility of text-to-3D generation using a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model. However, it struggles to generate high-resolution 3D content due to the limited resolution of the generated images and the inefficiency of the NeRF representation. We present Magic3D, a two-stage optimization framework that generates high-resolution 3D content from text descriptions. In the first stage, we use a low-resolution diffusion model to optimize a coarse NeRF representation. In the second stage, we use a high-resolution diffusion model to optimize a textured 3D mesh, initialized from the coarse NeRF. This two-stage approach allows us to generate 3D content at 512x512 resolution, which is significantly higher than the 64x64 resolution achieved by DreamFusion. We demonstrate that Magic3D can generate high-quality 3D content from a wide variety of text descriptions, and that the generated content can be rendered in real-time.

title: Point-E: A System for Generating 3D Point Clouds from Complex Prompts
abstract: We present Point-E, a system for generating 3D point clouds from complex text prompts. Point-E uses a two-stage approach: first, it generates an image from the text prompt using a text-to-image diffusion model; then, it generates a 3D point cloud from the image using a conditional point cloud diffusion model. We train the point cloud diffusion model on a large dataset of 3D objects and their rendered images, and show that it can generalize to generate point clouds from novel text prompts. Point-E can generate 3D point clouds in a matter of seconds on a single GPU, making it significantly faster than prior text-to-3D approaches that require hours of optimization per sample. We evaluate Point-E on a variety of text prompts and show that it can generate diverse, high-quality 3D point clouds that match the text descriptions.

title: Shap-E: Generating Conditional 3D Implicit Functions
abstract: We present Shap-E, a conditional generative model for 3D implicit functions. Shap-E can directly generate the parameters of implicit functions that represent 3D shapes, rather than generating point clouds or meshes. We train Shap-E on a large dataset of 3D assets and their text descriptions, and show that it can generate high-quality 3D shapes from text prompts. Shap-E uses a transformer-based diffusion model to generate the parameters of a neural network that represents the 3D shape. We show that Shap-E can generate diverse, high-quality 3D shapes that match the text descriptions, and that the generated shapes can be rendered and used in downstream applications. We also show that Shap-E can be used to generate 3D shapes from images, by conditioning the diffusion model on image features.

title: DiffWave: A Versatile Diffusion Model for Audio Synthesis
abstract: We present DiffWave, a versatile diffusion probabilistic model for waveform generation. DiffWave is a non-autoregressive model that can generate high-quality audio waveforms by iteratively refining noise. We show that DiffWave achieves competitive results on several text-to-speech benchmarks, with quality comparable to strong autoregressive models like WaveNet and WaveRNN. DiffWave can also be used for unconditional waveform generation, achieving state-of-the-art results on the unconditional speech generation task. In addition, DiffWave can be used for voice conversion and speaker adaptation, by conditioning the diffusion process on speaker embeddings. DiffWave is faster than autoregressive models during inference, as it can generate waveforms in parallel.

title: WaveNet: A Generative Model for Raw Audio
abstract: This paper introduces WaveNet, a deep generative model of raw audio waveforms. We show that WaveNets are able to generate speech which mimics any human voice and which sounds more natural than the best existing text-to-speech systems, reducing the gap with human performance by over 50% for both US English and Mandarin Chinese. A single WaveNet can generate speech that sounds more natural than the best existing text-to-speech systems, while also being capable of playing different musical instruments, generating realistic bird sounds, and generating other complex audio waveforms. We also demonstrate that the same model can be used for music generation and speech recognition.

title: Jukebox: A Generative Model for Music
abstract: We introduce Jukebox, a model that generates music with singing in the raw audio domain. We tackle the long context of raw audio using a multi-scale approach in which we autoencode raw audio to a lower sample rate via a convolutional neural network, and then model the resulting codes using Transformers. We show that the combined model at scale can generate high-fidelity and diverse songs with coherence up to multiple minutes. We can condition on artist and genre to steer the musical and vocal style, and on unaligned lyrics to make the singing more controllable. We release thousands of non cherry-picked samples on our website, along with model weights and code.

title: MusicLM: Generating Music from Text
abstract: We introduce MusicLM, a model for generating high-fidelity music from text descriptions. MusicLM is a hierarchical sequence-to-sequence model that generates music at 24 kHz using a cascade of autoregressive models. The model is trained on a large dataset of music and their text descriptions, and can generate music that is up to several minutes long. We demonstrate that MusicLM can generate music that is both diverse and high-quality, and that it can be conditioned on a wide variety of text descriptions, including genre, mood, instrumentation, and tempo. We also show that MusicLM can be used for other music generation tasks, such as melody continuation and music infilling.

title: AudioLDM: Text-to-Audio Generation with Latent Diffusion Models
abstract: Text-to-audio (TTA) generation has recently attracted significant interest. However, previous approaches have been limited by the quality and diversity of the generated audio. We present AudioLDM, a TTA generation system that uses latent diffusion models to generate high-quality audio from text descriptions. AudioLDM learns continuous audio representations from contrastive language-audio pretraining (CLAP) latents, which enables it to generate audio that is both semantically aligned with the text description and acoustically plausible. AudioLDM achieves state-of-the-art TTA generation performance on several benchmarks, and can also be used for text-guided audio style transfer, super-resolution, and inpainting. We release the model and code to facilitate future research.

title: Noise2Music: Text-conditioned Music Generation with Diffusion Models
abstract: We present Noise2Music, a system for generating music from text descriptions using diffusion models. Noise2Music uses a cascade of diffusion models to generate music at multiple resolutions, starting from a low-resolution latent representation and progressively upsampling to the final audio waveform. We train the model on a large dataset of music and their text descriptions, and show that it can generate high-quality music that matches the text descriptions. We also show that Noise2Music can be used for music editing tasks like inpainting and style transfer, and that it can generate music in a variety of genres and styles.

title: Moûsai: Text-to-Music Generation with Long-Context Latent Diffusion
abstract: We present Moûsai, a text-to-music generation system that uses latent diffusion models to generate long musical pieces. Moûsai uses a hierarchical approach to generate music, first generating a low-resolution latent representation and then upsampling it to the final audio waveform. We introduce a new architecture for the diffusion model that can handle long sequences, and a new conditioning mechanism that allows the model to generate music that is both diverse and coherent. We evaluate Moûsai on a variety of text-to-music benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results. We also show that Moûsai can generate music that is up to several minutes long, and that it can be conditioned on a wide variety of text descriptions.

title: Stable Audio: Fast Timing-Conditioned Latent Audio Diffusion
abstract: We present Stable Audio, a latent diffusion model for audio generation that is conditioned on text metadata and audio file duration. Stable Audio uses a highly downsampled latent representation of audio, which enables it to generate high-quality audio in a fraction of the time required by prior diffusion models. We train the model on a large dataset of licensed music and sound effects, and show that it can generate a wide variety of audio content, including music, sound effects, and ambient sounds. Stable Audio can generate audio of variable length, from a few seconds to several minutes, and can be conditioned on text descriptions to control the content and style of the generated audio. We release the model weights and inference code to the research community.

title: Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: We argue that the theory and practice of diffusion-based generative models are currently unnecessarily convoluted and seek to remedy the situation by presenting a design space that clearly separates the concrete design choices. This lets us identify several changes to both the sampling and training processes, as well as preconditioning of the score networks. Our redesign yields improved performance in terms of sample quality and likelihood, as well as faster sampling. We also rederive the previous diffusion models from our point of view, and analyze the design choices they implicitly made. We improve the state-of-the-art FID of 2.27 on unconditional CIFAR-10 to 1.79, and on ImageNet 64x64 from 2.01 to 1.52. On ImageNet 256x256, we improve the state-of-the-art FID from 4.59 to 2.44.

title: DPM-Solver: A Fast ODE Solver for Diffusion Probabilistic Model Sampling in Around 10 Steps
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality samples, but their sampling process requires solving a diffusion stochastic differential equation (SDE) or ordinary differential equation (ODE), which can be slow. We propose DPM-Solver, a fast ODE solver specifically designed for diffusion probabilistic models. DPM-Solver uses a high-order solver for the diffusion ODE that requires only a small number of function evaluations (around 10) to generate high-quality samples. DPM-Solver is based on the following key insights: first, the diffusion ODE can be solved more efficiently using a semi-linear structure; second, the score function can be approximated more accurately using a high-order Taylor expansion; and third, the solver can be stabilized using a novel corrector step. We evaluate DPM-Solver on several image generation benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art sampling speed while maintaining high sample quality.

title: DPM-Solver++: Fast Solver for Guided Sampling of Diffusion Probabilistic Models
abstract: Guided sampling is a key technique for controlling the generation process of diffusion probabilistic models, enabling applications like text-to-image generation and image editing. However, existing fast ODE solvers for diffusion models are designed for unconditional sampling and do not work well with guided sampling. We propose DPM-Solver++, a fast solver specifically designed for guided sampling of diffusion probabilistic models. DPM-Solver++ extends DPM-Solver to handle the additional guidance term, and introduces several improvements that make it more stable and efficient for guided sampling. We evaluate DPM-Solver++ on several guided sampling benchmarks, including classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results with only 10-20 function evaluations.

title: Progressive Distillation for Fast Sampling of Diffusion Models
abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable success in generating high-quality samples, but their iterative sampling process is slow and limits real-time applications. We present progressive distillation, a method for distilling a pretrained diffusion model into a model that requires fewer sampling steps. Progressive distillation works by repeatedly halving the number of required sampling steps, each time distilling the model into a new model that requires half as many steps. We show that progressive distillation can reduce the number of sampling steps from hundreds to as few as 4, while maintaining high sample quality. We also show that progressive distillation can be combined with other acceleration techniques like DPM-Solver to further improve sampling speed.

title: Score Jacobian Chaining: Lifting Pretrained 2D Diffusion Models for 3D Generation
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: We introduce Score Jacobian Chaining (SJC), a method for using pretrained 2D diffusion models to generate 3D objects. SJC uses the diffusion model to provide a score function that guides the optimization of a 3D representation. Unlike prior work that requires training a separate 3D diffusion model, SJC leverages the rich priors learned by 2D diffusion models to generate 3D objects without any 3D training data. We show that SJC can generate high-quality 3D objects from text descriptions, and that it can be used for a variety of 3D generation tasks, including text-to-3D, image-to-3D, and 3D editing. We also show that SJC is more efficient than prior work, as it does not require expensive 3D rendering during training.

title: Photorealistic Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Deep Language Understanding
abstract: We present Imagen, a text-to-image diffusion model with an unprecedented degree of photorealism and a deep level of language understanding. Imagen builds on the power of large transformer language models in understanding text and hinges on the strength of diffusion models in high-fidelity image generation. Our key discovery is that generic large language models (e.g., T5), pretrained on text-only corpora, are surprisingly effective at encoding text for image synthesis: increasing the size of the language model in Imagen boosts both sample fidelity and image-text alignment much more than increasing the size of the image diffusion model. Imagen achieves a new state-of-the-art FID score of 7.27 on the COCO dataset, without ever training on COCO, and human raters find Imagen samples to be on par with the COCO data itself in terms of image-text alignment.

title: Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
abstract: We present ControlNet, a neural network architecture that adds spatial conditioning controls to large, pretrained text-to-image diffusion models. ControlNet locks the parameters of a large pretrained diffusion model and duplicates its encoding layers into a trainable copy. The trainable copy is connected to the locked model via zero convolution layers, which initially output zeros and thus do not affect the pretrained model. The trainable copy is conditioned on additional control inputs, such as edge maps, depth maps, or human poses, and learns to generate images that are consistent with both the text prompt and the control input. We show that ControlNet can be used to add a wide variety of controls to pretrained text-to-image models, and that it achieves competitive results with prior work on controllable image generation. We release the model weights and code to the research community.

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
abstract: The dominant paradigm for adapting large language models to downstream tasks is fine-tuning all the parameters of the model. However, this approach is computationally expensive and requires storing a full copy of the model for each task. We present LoRA, a low-rank adaptation approach that freezes the pretrained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture. LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks by 10,000x, and reduces the GPU memory requirement by 3x. LoRA performs on-par or better than fine-tuning on several benchmarks, despite having far fewer trainable parameters. We also show that LoRA can be combined with other parameter-efficient adaptation methods like prefix tuning to further improve performance.

title: An Image is Worth One Word: Personalizing Text-to-Image Generation using Textual Inversion
abstract: Text-to-image models offer unprecedented freedom to guide creation through natural language. However, it is unclear how such freedom can be exercised to generate images of specific unique concepts, modify their appearance, or compose them in new roles and novel scenes. In other words, we ask: how can we use language-guided models to turn our cat into a painting, or imagine a new product based on our favorite toy? Here we present a simple approach that allows such creative freedom. Using only 3-5 images of a user-provided concept, we learn to represent it through new ''words'' in the embedding space of a frozen text-to-image model. These ''words'' can be composed into natural language sentences, guiding personalized creation in an intuitive way. We validate our approach on a variety of tasks, including subject-driven generation, style transfer, and concept composition.

title: DreamBooth: Fine Tuning Text-to-Image Diffusion Models for Subject-Driven Generation
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: Large text-to-image models have achieved remarkable success in allowing users to generate images in a variety of styles. However, it is still a challenge to generate images of a specific subject in a variety of poses, lighting conditions, and contexts. We present DreamBooth, a method for ''personalizing'' a text-to-image diffusion model by fine-tuning it on a small set of images of a specific subject. DreamBooth uses a rare token to represent the subject, and fine-tunes the model to generate images of the subject in a variety of contexts. We show that DreamBooth can generate high-quality, diverse images of the subject, and that it can be used for a variety of applications, including subject-driven generation, style transfer, and concept composition. We also show that DreamBooth can be used to generate images of multiple subjects in a single scene.

title: InstructPix2Pix: Learning to Follow Image Editing Instructions
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: We present InstructPix2Pix, a method for editing images from human instructions. Given an input image and a written instruction, our model follows the instruction to edit the image. To obtain training data, we combine the knowledge of two large pretrained models -- a language model (GPT-3) and a text-to-image model (Stable Diffusion) -- to generate a large dataset of image editing examples. Our conditional diffusion model, InstructPix2Pix, is trained on this generated data, and generalizes to real images and user-written instructions at inference time. We demonstrate that InstructPix2Pix can perform a wide variety of image editing tasks, including style transfer, object replacement, and scene modification, all from natural language instructions.

title: Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers
venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
abstract: We present Diffusion Transformers (DiT), a new architecture for diffusion models that replaces the traditional U-Net backbone with a transformer. We train DiT models on latent diffusion models (LDMs) and show that DiT achieves competitive results with U-Net-based models on image generation benchmarks. We also show that DiT scales more effectively than U-Net, with larger models achieving better performance. We investigate several design choices for DiT, including the patch size, the depth and width of the transformer, and the use of adaptive layer normalization. We find that DiT with adaptive layer normalization and a patch size of 2 achieves the best results. Our largest DiT model achieves an FID of 2.27 on ImageNet 256x256, which is competitive with the state of the art.

title: Visual Autoregressive Modeling: Scalable Image Generation via Next-Scale Prediction
abstract: We present Visual Autoregressive Modeling (VAR), a new class of autoregressive generative models for images. Unlike traditional autoregressive models that generate images pixel-by-pixel or token-by-token, VAR generates images in a coarse-to-fine manner, predicting the next scale of an image given the previous scales. This approach allows VAR to generate high-resolution images more efficiently than traditional autoregressive models. We train VAR on ImageNet at multiple resolutions and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results on image generation benchmarks. VAR also exhibits better scaling behavior than diffusion transformers, with performance improving more rapidly as the model size increases. We also show that VAR can be used for a variety of downstream tasks, including image classification, segmentation, and depth estimation.

title: MUSE: Text-To-Image Generation via Masked Generative Transformers
abstract: We present MUSE, a text-to-image generation model based on masked generative transformers. MUSE uses a transformer architecture to predict masked image tokens in parallel, conditioned on a text prompt. Unlike autoregressive models that predict tokens one at a time, MUSE can predict multiple tokens in parallel, which significantly speeds up generation. We train MUSE on a large dataset of images and their text descriptions, and show that it achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art text-to-image models like Imagen and DALL-E 2. MUSE can generate high-quality images from text descriptions in a matter of seconds, making it significantly faster than autoregressive models. We also show that MUSE can be used for image editing tasks like inpainting and outpainting.

title: Repaint: Inpainting using Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: Free-form inpainting is the task of adding new content to an image in the regions specified by an arbitrary binary mask. Most existing approaches train specialized models for this task, which operate only on fixed resolutions and need to be retrained for each task when the generation rules change. In this work, we take advantage of the generalization capabilities of pretrained unconditional diffusion probabilistic models to solve the inpainting problem. We use a resampling technique that iteratively denoises the output while conditioning on the known pixels using the posterior probability. We do not need to train or modify the original model. Our method can be used with any pretrained unconditional diffusion model. We evaluate our approach on several challenging benchmarks and achieve state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing methods that were specifically trained for the inpainting task.

title: Blended Diffusion for Text-driven Editing of Natural Images
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: We present Blended Diffusion, a method for text-driven editing of natural images. Blended Diffusion uses a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model to edit an image according to a text description. The key idea is to blend the diffusion process of the original image with the diffusion process of the edited image, allowing the model to preserve the structure of the original image while changing its appearance according to the text description. We show that Blended Diffusion can perform a wide variety of editing tasks, including object replacement, style transfer, and scene modification. We also show that Blended Diffusion outperforms prior work on text-driven image editing, and that it can be used to edit high-resolution images.

title: Null-text Inversion for Editing Real Images using Guided Diffusion Models
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: Recent large-scale text-guided diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable results in image synthesis. Editing real images using these models, however, remains a challenge. A promising approach is to first invert the image to latent noise, and then edit the latent using text guidance. However, standard inversion techniques do not work well for real images, as they often introduce artifacts or fail to preserve the details of the original image. We present null-text inversion, a method for inverting real images to latent noise that is compatible with classifier-free guided diffusion models. Our key insight is that the unconditional prediction in classifier-free guidance can be optimized to better reconstruct the input image, without changing the text-conditioned prediction. This allows us to invert real images with high fidelity, and then edit them using text guidance. We demonstrate that null-text inversion enables high-quality editing of real images, including style transfer, object replacement, and scene modification.

title: Prompt-to-Prompt Image Editing with Cross Attention Control
abstract: Recent large-scale text-to-image diffusion models have demonstrated an unprecedented ability to generate high-quality images from text prompts. However, editing these images in a controlled way remains a challenge. We present Prompt-to-Prompt, a method for editing images generated by text-to-image diffusion models by modifying only the text prompt. Our key insight is that the cross-attention layers in the diffusion model provide a strong connection between the text tokens and the spatial regions of the generated image. By controlling the cross-attention maps, we can control which regions of the image are affected by which text tokens. This allows us to perform a wide variety of editing operations, including word replacement, style transfer, and object manipulation, all by modifying only the text prompt. We demonstrate that Prompt-to-Prompt enables precise and intuitive editing of generated images, and that it can be used to edit real images using an inversion technique.

title: DeepFloyd IF: A Modular Cascade of Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Generation
abstract: We present DeepFloyd IF, a state-of-the-art text-to-image cascade of multiple diffusion models that progressively generate images of increasing resolution. DeepFloyd IF consists of three stages: a base diffusion model that generates a low-resolution image (64x64) from a text prompt, a series of super-resolution diffusion models that upsample the image to higher resolutions (256x256 and 1024x1024), and a final diffusion model that adds fine details. The base model is trained on a large dataset of images and their text descriptions, and uses a frozen text encoder (T5-XXL) to encode the text prompt. The super-resolution models are trained on pairs of low-resolution and high-resolution images. We show that DeepFloyd IF achieves state-of-the-art results on image generation benchmarks, with particularly strong performance on text-image alignment and image quality.

title: Encoding in Style: a StyleGAN Encoder for Image-to-Image Translation
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: We present a generic image-to-image translation framework, pixel2style2pixel (pSp), based on a novel encoder network that directly generates a series of style vectors which are fed into a pretrained StyleGAN generator. The pSp framework is based on a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) over a ResNet backbone, followed by a mapping network that produces style vectors. We show that this simple architecture can be used for a wide variety of image-to-image translation tasks, including face frontalization, conditional face synthesis, and super-resolution. We also show that pSp achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods on these tasks, while being significantly simpler and faster. The key advantage of pSp is that it can leverage the rich prior learned by StyleGAN, which enables it to generate high-quality images even from challenging inputs.

title: GAN Inversion: A Survey
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: GAN inversion aims to invert a given image back into the latent space of a pretrained GAN model, enabling the manipulation of real images using the generator. This task is challenging because the latent space of a GAN is often high-dimensional and non-linear, and the mapping from latent codes to images is many-to-one. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive overview of GAN inversion methods, categorizing them into optimization-based, encoder-based, and hybrid approaches. We also discuss the applications of GAN inversion, including image editing, image restoration, and image generation. We compare the different approaches on several benchmarks and discuss their strengths and weaknesses. We also identify open problems and future directions in GAN inversion research.

title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
abstract: State-of-the-art computer vision systems are trained to predict a fixed set of predetermined object categories. This restricted form of supervision limits their generality and usability since additional labeled data is needed to specify any other visual concept. Learning directly from raw text about images is a promising alternative which leverages a much broader source of supervision. We demonstrate that the simple pre-training task of predicting which caption goes with which image is an efficient and scalable way to learn SOTA image representations from scratch on a dataset of 400 million (image, text) pairs collected from the internet. After pre-training, natural language is used to reference learned visual concepts (or describe new ones) enabling zero-shot transfer of the model to downstream tasks.

title: Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Classification
abstract: We show that diffusion models can be used for image classification, achieving competitive results with state-of-the-art classifiers. We use a pretrained diffusion model to extract features from images, and then train a linear classifier on top of these features. We show that the features extracted by diffusion models are highly discriminative, and that they can be used for a variety of classification tasks. We also show that diffusion models can be used for few-shot classification, by using the diffusion process to generate additional training data. Our results suggest that diffusion models are a promising approach for image classification, and that they may offer advantages over traditional classifiers in certain settings.

title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
abstract: How can we perform efficient inference and learning in directed probabilistic models, in the presence of continuous latent variables with intractable posterior distributions, and large datasets? We introduce a stochastic variational inference and learning algorithm that scales to large datasets and, under some mild differentiability conditions, even works in the intractable case. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we show that a reparameterization of the variational lower bound yields a lower bound estimator that can be straightforwardly optimized using standard stochastic gradient methods. Second, we show that for i.i.d. datasets with continuous latent variables per datapoint, posterior inference can be made especially efficient by fitting an approximate inference model (also called a recognition model) to the intractable posterior using the proposed lower bound estimator. We demonstrate the approach on a variety of generative models, including deep exponential family models and deep variational autoencoders.

title: Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows
abstract: The choice of approximate posterior distribution is one of the core problems in variational inference. In this work, we develop a new approach to variational inference that uses normalizing flows to define a flexible family of approximate posterior distributions. Normalizing flows are a sequence of invertible transformations that can be used to transform a simple base distribution into a complex distribution. We show that normalizing flows can be used to define arbitrarily complex approximate posterior distributions, and that they can be trained efficiently using stochastic gradient descent. We demonstrate the approach on a variety of tasks, including density estimation, generative modeling, and variational autoencoders. We show that normalizing flows achieve competitive results with state-of-the-art methods, while being more flexible and easier to train.

title: Density Estimation using Real NVP
abstract: Unsupervised learning of probabilistic models is a central yet challenging problem in machine learning. Specifically, designing models with tractable learning, sampling, inference and evaluation is crucial in solving that task. We extend the space of such models using real-valued non-volume preserving (real NVP) transformations, a set of powerful invertible and learnable transformations, resulting in an unsupervised learning algorithm with exact log-likelihood computation, exact sampling, exact inference of observed variables, and an interpretable latent space. We demonstrate its ability to model natural images on four datasets through sampling, log-likelihood evaluation, and latent variable manipulations.

title: Glow: Generative Flow with Invertible 1x1 Convolutions
abstract: Flow-based generative models (Dinh et al., 2014) are conceptually attractive due to tractability of the exact log-likelihood, tractability of exact latent-variable inference, and parallelizability of both training and synthesis. In this paper we propose Glow, a simple type of generative flow using an invertible 1x1 convolution. Using our method we demonstrate a significant improvement in log-likelihood on standard benchmarks. Perhaps most strikingly, we demonstrate that a generative model optimized towards the plain log-likelihood objective is capable of efficient realistic-looking synthesis and manipulation of large images. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/openai/glow.

title: Improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
abstract: We present several improvements to diffusion probabilistic models. We use a learned variance parameter in the reverse process, and find that this improves both log-likelihood and sample quality. We also investigate different parameterizations of the diffusion process, showing that a cosine noise schedule improves sample quality for high-resolution image generation. We further analyze the training process and show that better optimization of the training objective leads to better results. Our best model achieves state-of-the-art FID scores on unconditional CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64x64, and competitive results on ImageNet 128x128.

title: Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching
abstract: Many statistical models are only defined up to a normalization constant. This makes parameter estimation difficult since the normalization constant is often computationally expensive to evaluate. We propose a new parameter estimation method for such models, which does not require the computation of the normalization constant. The method is based on minimizing the expected squared distance between the gradient of the log-density (the score function) and the gradient of the log-density of the data. We show that this objective function can be estimated consistently from data, and that it leads to a computationally efficient estimation algorithm. We apply the method to several statistical models, including Markov random fields and independent component analysis, and show that it achieves competitive results with maximum likelihood estimation.

title: Sliced Score Matching: A Scalable Approach to Density and Score Estimation
abstract: Score matching (SM) and its variants are powerful methods for density estimation and score estimation, but their computational cost scales quadratically with the data dimension. We propose Sliced Score Matching (SSM), a scalable method for density and score estimation that uses random projections to reduce the dimensionality of the problem. SSM has a computational cost that scales linearly with the data dimension, making it suitable for high-dimensional problems. We show that SSM is a consistent estimator of the score function, and that it achieves competitive results with SM on several benchmarks. We also show that SSM can be used for training energy-based models and score-based generative models, and that it scales to high-dimensional image datasets.

title: Score-based Generative Modeling in Latent Space
abstract: Score-based generative models have demonstrated unprecedented results in density estimation and sample quality. However, the training and sampling of these models can be computationally expensive, especially for high-dimensional data. We propose Latent Score-based Generative Models (LSGM), a new class of score-based generative models that operates in a low-dimensional latent space. LSGM uses a variational autoencoder to map data to a low-dimensional latent space, and then trains a score-based model in the latent space. This significantly reduces the computational cost of both training and sampling. We show that LSGM achieves competitive results with score-based models that operate in the data space, while being significantly faster. We also show that LSGM can be used for a variety of downstream tasks, including image generation, interpolation, and manipulation.

title: Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge with Applications to Score-Based Generative Modeling
abstract: The Schrödinger bridge problem (SBP) is a classic problem in stochastic control that seeks to find a stochastic process that interpolates between two given distributions. In this paper, we show that the SBP has deep connections to score-based generative models, and that solving the SBP can be used to improve the training and sampling of these models. We propose a new algorithm for solving the SBP called Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF), which iteratively refines the forward and backward processes until convergence. We show that IPF can be used to train score-based generative models that achieve competitive results with state-of-the-art methods. We also show that the SBP provides a principled way to design diffusion processes for score-based models, and that it can be used to improve the sample quality and sampling speed of these models.

title: Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics
abstract: A central problem in machine learning involves modeling complex data-sets using highly flexible families of probability distributions in which learning, sampling, inference, and evaluation are still analytically or computationally tractable. Here, we develop an approach that simultaneously achieves both flexibility and tractability. The essential idea, inspired by non-equilibrium statistical physics, is to systematically and slowly destroy structure in a data distribution through an iterative forward diffusion process. We then learn a reverse diffusion process that restores structure in data, yielding a highly flexible and tractable generative model of the data. This approach allows us to rapidly learn, sample, and evaluate probabilities in deep generative models with thousands of layers or time steps, as well as to compute conditional and posterior probabilities under the learned model.

title: Semantic Image Synthesis with Spatially-Adaptive Normalization
abstract: We propose spatially-adaptive normalization, a simple but effective layer for synthesizing photorealistic images given an input semantic layout. Previous methods directly feed the semantic layout as input to the network, which is then processed through stacks of convolution, normalization, and nonlinearity layers. We show that this is suboptimal because the normalization layers tend to wash away semantic information. To address this issue, we propose using the input layout for modulating the activations in normalization layers through a spatially-adaptive, learned transformation. Experiments on several challenging datasets demonstrate that spatially-adaptive normalization leads to visually compelling results for a diverse range of scenes, including outdoor landscapes, interiors, and street scenes.

title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis and Semantic Manipulation with Conditional GANs
abstract: We present a method for synthesizing high-resolution photo-realistic images from semantic label maps using conditional generative adversarial networks (conditional GANs). Conditional GANs have enabled a variety of applications, but the results are often limited to low-resolution and still far from realistic. In this work, we generate 2048x1024 visually appealing results with a novel adversarial loss, as well as new multi-scale generator and discriminator architectures. Furthermore, we extend our framework to the interactive visual manipulation of both created photographic images and hand-drawn sketches. We propose a instance-wise feature embedding scheme, as well as a method for generating diverse results given the same input. Finally, we apply our approach to the photo-realistic image synthesis of street scenes, as well as the semantic editing of natural scenes.

title: SinGAN: Learning a Generative Model from a Single Natural Image
abstract: We introduce SinGAN, an unconditional generative model that can be learned from just a single natural image. Our model, trained using internal statistics of a single image, learns to generate diverse samples that capture the internal distribution of patches within the image. SinGAN uses a pyramid of fully convolutional GANs, each responsible for capturing the distribution of patches at a different scale. This allows SinGAN to generate new realistic images with arbitrary size and aspect ratio, that preserve the original patch distribution while exhibiting new object configurations and structures. SinGAN is widely applicable to a multitude of image manipulation tasks, including image harmonization, editing, super-resolution, and animation. In all these tasks, SinGAN produces high-quality results that outperform prior work, despite being trained on a single image.

title: Photo-Realistic Single Image Super-Resolution Using a Generative Adversarial Network
abstract: Despite the breakthroughs in accuracy and speed of single image super-resolution using faster and deeper convolutional neural networks, one central problem remains largely unsolved: how do we recover the finer texture details when we super-resolve at large upscaling factors? The behavior of optimization-based super-resolution methods is principally driven by the choice of the objective function. Recent work has largely focused on minimizing the mean squared reconstruction error. The resulting estimates have high peak signal-to-noise ratios, but they are often lacking high-frequency details and are perceptually unsatisfying in the sense that they fail to match the fidelity expected at the higher resolution. In this paper, we present SRGAN, a generative adversarial network (GAN) for image super-resolution (SR). To our knowledge, it is the first framework capable of inferring photo-realistic natural images for 4x upscaling factors. To achieve this, we propose a perceptual loss function which consists of an adversarial loss and a content loss.

title: ESRGAN: Enhanced Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: The Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (SRGAN) is a seminal work that is capable of generating realistic textures during single image super-resolution. However, the hallucinated details in the super-resolved images usually appear with unpleasant artifacts. To further enhance the visual quality, we thoroughly study three key components of SRGAN - network architecture, adversarial loss and perceptual loss, and improve each of them to derive an Enhanced SRGAN (ESRGAN). In particular, we introduce the Residual-in-Residual Dense Block (RRDB) without batch normalization as the basic network building unit. Moreover, we borrow the idea from relativistic GAN to let the discriminator predict relative realness instead of the absolute value. Finally, we improve the perceptual loss by using the features before activation, which could provide stronger supervision for brightness consistency and texture recovery. Benefiting from these improvements, the proposed ESRGAN achieves consistently better visual quality with more realistic and natural textures than SRGAN and won the first place in the PIRM2018-SR Challenge.

title: U-GAT-IT: Unsupervised Generative Attentional Networks with Adaptive Layer-Instance Normalization for Image-to-Image Translation
abstract: We propose a novel method for unsupervised image-to-image translation, which incorporates a new attention module and a new learnable normalization function in an end-to-end manner. The attention module guides our model to focus on more important regions distinguishing between source and target domains based on the attention map obtained by the auxiliary classifier. Unlike previous attention-based methods which cannot handle the geometric changes between domains, our model can translate both images requiring holistic changes and images requiring large shape changes. Our model also outperforms the previous state-of-the-art models in terms of visual quality and translation accuracy. We further propose a new normalization function called Adaptive Layer-Instance Normalization (AdaLIN), which adaptively selects the normalization method based on the content and style of the input image.

title: Image Style Transfer Using Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: Rendering the semantic content of an image in different styles is a difficult image processing task. Arguably, a major limiting factor for previous approaches has been the lack of image representations that explicitly represent semantic information and, thus, allow to separate image content from style. Here we use image representations derived from Convolutional Neural Networks optimised for object recognition, which make high level image information explicit. We introduce A Neural Algorithm of Artistic Style that can separate and recombine the image content and style of natural images. The algorithm allows us to produce new images of high perceptual quality that combine the content of an arbitrary photograph with the appearance of numerous well-known artworks. Our results provide new insights into the deep image representations learned by Convolutional Neural Networks and demonstrate their potential for high level image synthesis and manipulation.

title: Arbitrary Style Transfer in Real-time with Adaptive Instance Normalization
abstract: Gatys et al. recently introduced a neural algorithm that renders a content image in the style of another image, achieving so-called style transfer. However, their framework requires a slow iterative optimization process, which limits its practical application. Fast approximations with feed-forward neural networks have been proposed to speed up neural style transfer. Unfortunately, the speed improvement comes at a cost: the network is usually tied to a fixed set of styles and cannot adapt to arbitrary new styles. In this paper, we present a simple yet effective approach that for the first time enables arbitrary style transfer in real-time. Our approach is based on Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN), a simple extension of instance normalization that aligns the mean and variance of the content features with those of the style features. AdaIN allows our network to transfer arbitrary styles in a single forward pass, while achieving comparable quality to the optimization-based approach.

title: Towards Faster and Stabilized GAN Training for High-fidelity Few-shot Synthesis
abstract: Training Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) with limited data (few-shot synthesis) is a challenging task. Existing approaches often suffer from training instability and mode collapse, especially when training on datasets with only a few hundred images. In this paper, we propose FastGAN, a method for faster and more stable GAN training on limited data. FastGAN uses a skip-layer excitation module and a self-supervised discriminator to improve training stability and sample quality. We show that FastGAN can generate high-fidelity images from datasets with as few as 100 images, and that it outperforms prior work on several few-shot synthesis benchmarks. We also show that FastGAN is significantly faster to train than prior work, achieving comparable results in a fraction of the training time.

title: Projected GANs Converge Faster
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis, but training them can be slow and unstable. We present Projected GANs, a method for faster and more stable GAN training. Projected GANs work by projecting the generated and real images into a lower-dimensional feature space before feeding them to the discriminator. This projection is learned during training, and it helps the discriminator focus on the most important features for distinguishing real from fake images. We show that Projected GANs converge significantly faster than standard GANs, and that they achieve comparable or better sample quality. We also show that Projected GANs are more stable to train, and that they can be used with a variety of GAN architectures.

title: StyleGAN-XL: Scaling StyleGAN to Large Diverse Datasets
abstract: Even though recent generative models have shown remarkable results on large-scale datasets, training on such datasets is challenging due to the computational cost and the need for careful hyperparameter tuning. We present StyleGAN-XL, a method for scaling StyleGAN to large, diverse datasets. StyleGAN-XL uses a combination of techniques to improve training efficiency and stability, including a new discriminator architecture, a new training objective, and a new data augmentation strategy. We show that StyleGAN-XL can be trained on ImageNet at 256x256 resolution in a matter of days on a single GPU, achieving state-of-the-art results. We also show that StyleGAN-XL scales well to larger datasets and higher resolutions, and that it can be used to generate high-quality images from a wide variety of domains.

title: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks
abstract: We present a scalable approach for semi-supervised learning on graph-structured data that is based on an efficient variant of convolutional neural networks which operate directly on graphs. Our approach induces hidden layer representations that encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. The proposed method demonstrates state-of-the-art classification results on a number of benchmark dataset tests.

title: Graph Attention Networks
abstract: We present graph attention networks (GATs), novel neural network architectures that operate on graph-structured data, leveraging masked self-attentional layers to address the shortcomings of prior methods based on graph convolutions or their approximations. By stacking layers in which nodes are able to attend over their neighborhoods' features, we enable (implicitly) specifying different weights to different nodes in a neighborhood, without requiring any kind of costly matrix operation (such as inversion) or depending on knowing the graph structure upfront. In this way, we address several key challenges of spectral-based graph neural networks simultaneously, and make our model readily applicable to inductive as well as transductive problems. Our GAT models have achieved or matched state-of-the-art results across four established transductive and inductive graph benchmarks: the Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed citation network datasets, as well as a protein-protein interaction dataset (wherein test graphs remain unseen during training).

title: Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Low-dimensional embeddings of nodes in large graphs have proved extremely useful in a variety of prediction tasks, from content recommendation to identifying protein functions. However, most existing approaches require that all nodes in the graph are present during training of the embeddings; these previous approaches are inherently transductive and do not naturally generalize to unseen nodes. Here we present GraphSAGE, a general inductive framework that leverages node feature information (e.g., text attributes) to efficiently generate node embeddings for previously unseen data. Instead of training individual embeddings for each node, we learn a function that generates embeddings by sampling and aggregating features from a node's local neighborhood. Our algorithm outperforms strong baselines on three inductive node-classification benchmarks: we classify the category of unseen nodes in evolving information graphs based on citation and Reddit post data, and we show that our algorithm generalizes to completely unseen graphs using a multi-graph dataset of protein-protein interactions.

title: How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks?
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an effective framework for representation learning of graphs. GNNs follow a neighborhood aggregation scheme, where the representation vector of a node is computed by recursively aggregating and transforming representation vectors of its neighboring nodes. Many GNN variants have been proposed and have achieved state-of-the-art results on both node and graph classification tasks. However, despite GNNs revolutionizing graph representation learning, there is limited understanding of their representational properties and limitations. Here, we present a theoretical framework for analyzing the expressive power of GNNs to capture different graph structures. Our results characterize the discriminative power of popular GNN variants, such as Graph Convolutional Networks and GraphSAGE, and show that they cannot learn to distinguish certain simple graph structures. We then develop a simple architecture that is provably the most expressive among the class of GNNs and is as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test. We empirically validate our theoretical findings on a number of graph classification benchmarks, and demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry
abstract: Supervised learning on molecules has incredible potential to be useful in chemistry, drug discovery, and materials science. Luckily, a number of relevant chemical tasks have come with benchmark data, including: quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, and biophysics datasets. To work on these datasets, we need to develop methods that utilize the rich information in the 3D structure of molecules. In this paper, we propose a general framework for generating representations of molecules using neural message passing. Our Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) encompass a broad class of existing methods for graph-structured data, and we demonstrate that many existing methods can be viewed as specific instantiations of MPNNs. We explore the design space of MPNNs on a large set of molecular properties datasets, and show that the best MPNN achieves state-of-the-art results on nearly all datasets, even compared to methods with complex task-specific architectures.

title: DeepWalk: Online Learning of Social Representations
venue: Proceedings of the 20th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
abstract: We present DeepWalk, a novel approach for learning latent representations of vertices in a network. These latent representations encode social relations in a continuous vector space, which is easily exploited by statistical models. DeepWalk generalizes recent advancements in language modeling and unsupervised feature learning (or deep learning) from sequences of words to graphs. DeepWalk uses local information obtained from truncated random walks to learn latent representations by treating walks as the equivalent of sentences. We demonstrate DeepWalk's latent representations on several multi-label network classification tasks for social networks such as BlogCatalog, Flickr, and YouTube. Our results show that DeepWalk outperforms challenging baselines which are allowed a global view of the network, especially in the presence of missing information. DeepWalk's representations can provide F1 scores up to 10% higher than competing methods when labeled data is sparse. In some experiments, DeepWalk's representations are able to outperform all baseline methods while using 60% less training data. DeepWalk is also scalable. It is an online learning algorithm which builds useful incremental results, and is trivially parallelizable. These qualities make it suitable for a broad class of real world applications such as network classification, and anomaly detection.

title: node2vec: Scalable Feature Learning for Networks
venue: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
abstract: Prediction tasks over nodes and edges in networks require careful effort in engineering features used by learning algorithms. Recent research in the broader field of representation learning has led to significant progress in automating prediction by learning the features themselves. However, present feature learning approaches are not expressive enough to capture the diversity of connectivity patterns observed in networks. Here we propose node2vec, an algorithmic framework for learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks. In node2vec, we learn a mapping of nodes to a low-dimensional space of features that maximizes the likelihood of preserving network neighborhoods of nodes. We define a flexible notion of a node's network neighborhood and design a biased random walk procedure, which efficiently explores diverse neighborhoods. Our algorithm generalizes prior work which is based on rigid notions of network neighborhoods, and we argue that the added flexibility in exploring neighborhoods is the key to learning richer representation. We demonstrate the efficacy of node2vec over existing state-of-the-art techniques on multi-label classification and link prediction in several real-world networks from diverse domains. Taken together, our work represents a new way for efficiently learning state-of-the-art task-independent representations in complex networks.

title: Modeling Relational Data with Graph Convolutional Networks
abstract: Knowledge graphs enable a wide variety of applications, including question answering and information retrieval. Despite the great effort invested in their creation and maintenance, even the largest (e.g., Yago, DBPedia or Wikidata) remain incomplete. We introduce Relational Graph Convolutional Networks (R-GCNs) and apply them to two standard knowledge base completion tasks: Link prediction (recovery of missing facts, i.e., subject-predicate-object triples) and entity classification (recovery of missing entity attributes).
