R-GCNs are related to a recent class of neural networks operating on graphs, and are developed specifically to deal with the highly multi-relational data characteristics of realistic knowledge bases. We demonstrate the effectiveness of R-GCNs as a stand-alone model for entity classification. We further show that factorization models for link prediction such as DistMult can be significantly improved by enriching them with an encoder model to accumulate evidence over multiple inference steps in the relational graph, demonstrating a large improvement of 29.8% on FB15k-237 over a decoder-only baseline.

title: Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Multi-relational data, involving multiple types of relationships between entities, is a common feature of many real-world applications such as recommender systems, social networks, and knowledge bases. In this paper, we propose a method for learning representations of multi-relational data that is based on the idea of representing entities as points in a low-dimensional vector space and relations as translations between these points. This approach, which we call TransE, allows us to model multi-relational data in a simple and efficient way. We evaluate TransE on a number of benchmark datasets for knowledge base completion, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. TransE is also computationally efficient, making it suitable for large-scale applications.

title: RotatE: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Relational Rotation in Complex Space
abstract: We study the problem of learning representations of entities and relations in knowledge graphs for predicting missing links. The success of such a task heavily relies on the ability of modeling and inferring the patterns of (or between) the relations. In this paper, we present a new approach for knowledge graph embedding called RotatE, which is able to model and infer various relation patterns including: symmetry/antisymmetry, inversion, and composition. Specifically, the RotatE model defines each relation as a rotation from the source entity to the target entity in the complex vector space. In addition, we propose a novel self-adversarial negative sampling technique for efficiently and effectively training the RotatE model. Experimental results on multiple benchmark knowledge graphs show that the proposed RotatE model is not only scalable, but also able to infer and model various relation patterns and significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art models for link prediction.

title: Complex Embeddings for Simple Link Prediction
abstract: The state of the art in modeling real-world knowledge graph data remains the simple multi-relational embedding model introduced by Bordes et al. (2013). In this paper, we introduce a new, more expressive variant of this model that makes use of complex-valued embeddings. Complex embeddings not only extend the model's representational capacity, but also naturally facilitate efficient and powerful scoring functions. We evaluate our ComplEx model on several benchmark datasets for link prediction in knowledge graphs and achieve state-of-the-art results on all datasets. We also show that our model can be efficiently computed on GPUs, making it suitable for large-scale applications. Our results suggest that complex-valued embeddings are a powerful tool for modeling multi-relational data, and that they offer a promising direction for future research in this area.

title: A Generalization of Transformer Networks to Graphs
venue: AAAI Workshop on Deep Learning on Graphs: Methods and Applications
abstract: We propose a generalization of transformer neural network architecture for arbitrary graphs. The original transformer was designed for Natural Language Processing (NLP), which operates on fully connected graphs representing all connections between the words in a sequence. Such architecture does not leverage the graph connectivity inductive bias, and can perform poorly when the graph topology is important and has not been encoded into the node features. We introduce a graph transformer with four new properties compared to the standard model. First, the attention mechanism is a function of the neighborhood connectivity for each node in the graph. Second, the positional encoding is represented by the Laplacian eigenvectors, which naturally generalize the sinusoidal positional encodings often used in NLP. Third, the layer normalization is replaced by a batch normalization layer, which provides faster training and better generalization performance. Finally, the architecture is extended to edge feature representation, which can be critical to tasks such as chemistry (bond type) or link prediction (entity relationship in knowledge graphs). Numerical experiments on a graph benchmark demonstrate the performance of the proposed graph transformer architecture.

title: LightGCN: Simplifying and Powering Graph Convolution Network for Recommendation
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval
abstract: Graph Convolution Network (GCN) has become a new state-of-the-art for collaborative filtering. Nevertheless, the reasons for its effectiveness for recommendation are not well understood. Existing work that adapts GCN to recommendation lacks thorough ablation analyses on GCN's two most common design elements -- feature transformation and nonlinear activation. In this paper, we argue that they are unnecessary for collaborative filtering and cause difficulties in training. We present LightGCN, which contains only the most essential component in GCN -- neighborhood aggregation -- for collaborative filtering. Specifically, LightGCN learns user and item embeddings by linearly propagating them on the user-item interaction graph, and uses the weighted sum of the embeddings learned at all layers as the final embedding. Such simple, linear, and neat model is easy to implement and efficient to train, and exhibits great predictive accuracy. We conduct extensive experiments on three public benchmarks and demonstrate the effectiveness of LightGCN, achieving significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

title: LINE: Large-scale Information Network Embedding
venue: Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on World Wide Web
abstract: This paper studies the problem of embedding very large information networks into low-dimensional vector spaces, which is useful in many tasks such as visualization, node classification, and link prediction. Most existing graph embedding methods do not scale for real world information networks which usually contain millions of nodes and billions of edges. In this work, we propose a novel network embedding method called the "LINE," which is suitable for arbitrary types of information networks: undirected, directed, and/or weighted. The method optimizes a carefully designed objective function that preserves both the local and global network structures. An edge-sampling algorithm is proposed that addresses the limitation of the classical stochastic gradient descent and improves both the effectiveness and the efficiency of the inference. Empirical experiments prove the effectiveness of the LINE on a variety of real-world information networks, including language networks, social networks, and citation networks. The algorithm is very efficient, which is able to learn the embedding of a network with millions of vertices and billions of edges in a few hours on a single machine.

title: Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network
abstract: Heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) have attracted increasing attention in recent years and demonstrated superior performance on various tasks. However, most existing methods typically focus on the meta-path guided neighborhood, which limits their ability to capture the full heterogeneity of the graph. In this paper, we propose a novel heterogeneous graph attention network (HAN) that is able to capture the rich semantic information in heterogeneous graphs. HAN utilizes node-level and semantic-level attention mechanisms to learn the importance of different meta-paths and nodes. The node-level attention mechanism learns the importance of different meta-path based neighbors for each node, while the semantic-level attention mechanism learns the importance of different meta-paths. By combining these two attention mechanisms, HAN is able to learn comprehensive node representations that capture the complex heterogeneity of the graph. We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world heterogeneous graphs and demonstrate that HAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various tasks, including node classification, node clustering, and link prediction.

title: Heterogeneous Graph Transformer
abstract: Heterogeneous graphs are ubiquitous in real-world applications, where nodes and edges can be of different types and carry different semantic meanings. Learning representations for heterogeneous graphs is challenging due to the complex structure and diverse semantics. In this paper, we propose the Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), a novel architecture for heterogeneous graph representation learning. HGT introduces the concept of meta-relation, which captures the relationship between different node and edge types. Based on meta-relations, HGT designs a parameter sharing strategy that allows the model to share parameters across different types of edges while still maintaining the ability to capture type-specific patterns. This parameter sharing strategy enables HGT to scale to large heterogeneous graphs with hundreds of millions of nodes and edges. We evaluate HGT on several large-scale heterogeneous graph benchmarks, including the Open Academic Graph, and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on various downstream tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph clustering.

title: Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning with Differentiable Pooling
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have revolutionized the field of graph representation learning through effectively learned node embeddings, and achieved state-of-the-art results in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. However, current GNN methods are inherently flat and do not learn hierarchical representations of graphs -- a limitation that is especially problematic for the task of graph classification, where the goal is to predict the label associated with an entire graph. Here we propose DiffPool, a differentiable graph pooling module that can generate hierarchical representations of graphs and can be combined with various graph neural network architectures in an end-to-end fashion. DiffPool learns a differentiable soft cluster assignment for nodes at each layer of a deep GNN, mapping nodes to a set of clusters, which then form the coarsened input for the next GNN layer. Our experimental results show that combining existing GNN methods with DiffPool yields an average improvement of 5-10% accuracy on graph classification benchmarks, compared to all existing pooling approaches, achieving a new state-of-the-art on four out of five benchmark datasets.

title: Deeper Insights into Graph Convolutional Networks for Semi-Supervised Learning
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have attracted significant research attention due to their promising performance in semi-supervised learning on graph-structured data. Despite their success, the behavior of GCNs is not well understood, and their performance degrades significantly when the network goes deeper. In this paper, we present a thorough analysis of GCNs and identify the limitations of existing GCN models. We find that the limitations of GCNs are mainly due to the limited expressive power of the graph convolutional layer, which acts as a Laplacian smoothing operator. This analysis provides new insights into GCNs and motivates us to develop a simple yet effective model, called Co-training and Self-training GCN (CS-GCN), which combines the strengths of GCNs with co-training and self-training methods. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CS-GCN achieves state-of-the-art performance on various semi-supervised learning benchmarks.

title: Representation Learning on Graphs with Jumping Knowledge Networks
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in learning representations for graph-structured data. A key component of GNNs is the neighborhood aggregation scheme, where the representation of each node is computed by recursively aggregating representations of its neighbors. However, different nodes may require different neighborhood ranges to best capture their structural and feature information. In this paper, we propose Jumping Knowledge (JK) Networks, a new architecture for GNNs that adaptively learns to aggregate information from different neighborhood ranges for each node. JK Networks use a jumping knowledge mechanism that allows each node to selectively aggregate representations from different layers, effectively learning the appropriate neighborhood range for each node. We demonstrate the effectiveness of JK Networks on various benchmarks, including social networks, citation networks, and molecular graphs, and show that they achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of tasks.

title: Graph U-Nets
venue: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of learning representations for graph data, where the goal is to learn a representation that captures both local and global structure of the graph. We propose Graph U-Nets, a new architecture for graph neural networks that is inspired by U-Net, a popular architecture for image segmentation. Graph U-Nets consist of an encoder and a decoder, where the encoder performs graph pooling operations to coarsen the graph, and the decoder performs graph unpooling operations to recover the original graph structure. We design a novel graph pooling operation called gPool, which adaptively selects a subset of nodes to form a coarsened graph, and a corresponding graph unpooling operation called gUnpool, which restores the original graph structure. We evaluate Graph U-Nets on various graph classification and node classification benchmarks, and demonstrate that they achieve state-of-the-art performance.

title: Self-Attention Graph Pooling
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, existing GNN models often struggle with graph-level tasks, such as graph classification, due to the lack of effective graph pooling operations. In this paper, we propose a novel graph pooling operation called Self-Attention Graph Pooling (SAGPool), which leverages self-attention mechanisms to select important nodes for graph-level representation learning. SAGPool computes attention scores for each node based on its features and the graph structure, and uses these scores to select a subset of nodes that form a coarsened graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SAGPool on various graph classification benchmarks, and show that it outperforms existing graph pooling methods.

title: Deep Graph Contrastive Representation Learning
venue: ICML Workshop on Graph Representation Learning and Beyond
abstract: Graph representation learning nowadays is ubiquitous in real-world applications, including recommendation systems, social network analysis, and drug discovery. However, existing methods often require abundant labeled data, which is expensive and time-consuming to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel graph contrastive learning framework called GRACE, which learns node representations by maximizing the agreement between different views of the same graph. GRACE constructs multiple views of a graph by applying different augmentation strategies, and then learns node representations by maximizing the similarity between the representations of the same node in different views. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GRACE on various semi-supervised and unsupervised node classification benchmarks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: InfoGraph: Unsupervised and Semi-supervised Graph-Level Representation Learning via Mutual Information Maximization
abstract: Learning representations for graph-structured data remains a challenging task, especially when labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. In this paper, we propose InfoGraph, a general framework for unsupervised and semi-supervised graph-level representation learning based on mutual information maximization. InfoGraph trains a graph neural network encoder to maximize the mutual information between the representations of entire graphs and the representations of substructures of different scales (e.g., nodes, edges, triangles). We demonstrate that InfoGraph achieves state-of-the-art performance on various graph classification benchmarks in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. We also show that InfoGraph can learn representations that capture the global structure of graphs, which is important for downstream tasks.

title: Link Prediction Based on Graph Neural Networks
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Link prediction is a key problem for graph-structured data, with applications in social network analysis, recommendation systems, and biological network analysis. Traditional link prediction methods rely on hand-crafted heuristics, which may not capture the complex patterns in real-world graphs. In this paper, we propose SEAL, a novel link prediction framework based on graph neural networks. SEAL extracts a local subgraph around each target link and uses a graph neural network to learn representations of the subgraph, which are then used to predict the existence of the link. We demonstrate that SEAL significantly outperforms existing link prediction methods on various benchmarks, including social networks, collaboration networks, and biological networks. We also show that SEAL can learn representations that capture the structural information of the local subgraph, which is crucial for accurate link prediction.

title: Variational Graph Auto-Encoders
venue: NIPS Workshop on Bayesian Deep Learning
abstract: We introduce the variational graph auto-encoder (VGAE), a framework for unsupervised learning on graph-structured data based on the variational auto-encoder (VAE). VGAE uses a graph neural network as an encoder to learn latent representations of nodes, and a simple inner product decoder to predict links between nodes. We demonstrate that VGAE achieves competitive results on the link prediction task, outperforming existing methods on several benchmark datasets. VGAE also has the advantage of being able to generate new graphs by sampling from the learned latent space, which can be useful for graph generation tasks. We further show that VGAE can be extended to incorporate node features, which improves its performance on tasks where node features are informative.

title: Modeling Relational Data with Graph Auto-Encoders
venue: NIPS Workshop on Bayesian Deep Learning
abstract: We study the problem of learning representations of relational data, such as knowledge graphs and social networks, using graph auto-encoders. We propose a simple and effective graph auto-encoder that uses a graph neural network as an encoder and an inner product decoder to predict links. We evaluate our model on the task of link prediction in knowledge graphs and social networks, and show that it achieves competitive results compared to existing methods. We also demonstrate that our model can be used for unsupervised learning of node representations, which can be useful for downstream tasks such as node classification and clustering.

title: SIGN: Scalable Inception Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, most existing GNN models suffer from scalability issues when dealing with large graphs, as they require the full graph Laplacian to be computed and stored in memory. In this paper, we propose SIGN, a scalable inception graph neural network that addresses these scalability issues. SIGN uses a fixed, deterministic graph diffusion process to precompute smoothed node features, which are then used as input to a standard neural network. This allows SIGN to scale to graphs with billions of edges while maintaining competitive performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SIGN on various large-scale graph benchmarks, including the Amazon2M and Reddit datasets, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being orders of magnitude faster than existing methods.

title: Cluster-GCN: An Efficient Algorithm for Training Deep and Large Graph Convolutional Networks
venue: Proceedings of the 25th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery & Data Mining
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, training deep and large GCNs remains a challenging task, as the memory and computational requirements grow rapidly with the size of the graph. In this paper, we propose Cluster-GCN, a novel algorithm for training deep and large GCNs efficiently. Cluster-GCN works by first clustering the graph into dense subgraphs, and then sampling these clusters to form mini-batches for training. This approach significantly reduces the number of neighbors that need to be considered during training, leading to substantial improvements in both memory and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Cluster-GCN on various large-scale graph benchmarks, including the Amazon2M, Reddit, and PPI datasets, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being orders of magnitude faster than existing methods.

title: FastGCN: Fast Learning with Graph Convolutional Networks via Importance Sampling
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, training GCNs on large graphs remains a challenging task due to the high computational cost of the graph convolution operation. In this paper, we propose FastGCN, a fast learning algorithm for GCNs based on importance sampling. FastGCN works by sampling a small subset of nodes for each training iteration, where the sampling probabilities are determined by the importance of each node. This approach significantly reduces the computational cost of training GCNs while maintaining competitive performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FastGCN on various large-scale graph benchmarks, including the Reddit and PPI datasets, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being orders of magnitude faster than existing methods.

title: GraphSAINT: Graph Sampling Based Inductive Learning Method
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, training GCNs on large graphs remains a challenging task due to the high computational cost of the graph convolution operation. In this paper, we propose GraphSAINT, a graph sampling based inductive learning method that addresses these scalability issues. GraphSAINT works by sampling subgraphs from the full graph during training, which significantly reduces the computational cost. We propose several sampling strategies, including node sampling, edge sampling, and random walk sampling, and analyze their theoretical properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GraphSAINT on various large-scale graph benchmarks, including the Reddit, Yelp, and Amazon datasets, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being orders of magnitude faster than existing methods.

title: TGAT: Inductive Representation Learning on Temporal Graphs
abstract: Temporal graphs, where edges are associated with timestamps, are ubiquitous in real-world applications such as social networks, financial transactions, and communication networks. Learning representations for temporal graphs is challenging due to the dynamic nature of the graph and the need to capture both structural and temporal information. In this paper, we propose TGAT, a novel inductive representation learning method for temporal graphs. TGAT uses a self-attention mechanism to aggregate information from temporal neighbors, and introduces a novel functional time encoding technique that captures the temporal information of the graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TGAT on various temporal graph benchmarks, including link prediction and node classification tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Temporal Graph Networks for Deep Learning on Dynamic Graphs
abstract: Graphs are a powerful representation for relational data, but most existing methods assume that the graph is static. However, many real-world graphs are dynamic, with nodes and edges appearing and disappearing over time. Learning representations for dynamic graphs is challenging due to the temporal nature of the data and the need to capture both structural and temporal patterns. In this paper, we propose Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs), a general framework for deep learning on dynamic graphs. TGNs use a memory module to store the state of each node at each time step, and a message passing mechanism to propagate information between nodes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TGNs on various dynamic graph benchmarks, including link prediction and node classification tasks, and show that they achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: DyRep: Learning Representations over Dynamic Graphs
abstract: Learning representations for dynamic graphs is a challenging task due to the temporal nature of the data and the need to capture both structural and temporal patterns. In this paper, we propose DyRep, a novel method for learning representations over dynamic graphs. DyRep uses a deep temporal point process model to capture the temporal dynamics of the graph, and a neural network to learn representations of nodes that evolve over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DyRep on various dynamic graph benchmarks, including link prediction and node classification tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: EvolveGCN: Evolving Graph Convolutional Networks for Dynamic Graphs
venue: Proceedings of the 29th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI)
abstract: Dynamic graphs, where nodes and edges can appear and disappear over time, are ubiquitous in real-world applications such as social networks, financial transactions, and communication networks. Learning representations for dynamic graphs is challenging due to the need to capture both structural and temporal patterns. In this paper, we propose EvolveGCN, a novel method for learning representations of dynamic graphs. EvolveGCN uses a recurrent neural network (RNN) to evolve the parameters of a graph convolutional network (GCN) over time, allowing the model to adapt to the changing graph structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EvolveGCN on various dynamic graph benchmarks, including link prediction and node classification tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Message Passing Neural Networks for Molecular Property Prediction
venue: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
abstract: Molecular property prediction is a fundamental task in chemistry and drug discovery, with applications in predicting molecular toxicity, solubility, and biological activity. Traditional methods for molecular property prediction rely on hand-crafted molecular descriptors, which may not capture the complex patterns in molecular structures. In this paper, we propose a message passing neural network (MPNN) framework for molecular property prediction. MPNNs operate directly on molecular graphs, learning representations of atoms and bonds through iterative message passing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MPNNs on a number of benchmark datasets for molecular property prediction, including the QM9 and ESOL datasets, and show that they achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Molecular Transformer: A Model for Accurate Calibrated Molecular Properties
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
abstract: Accurate prediction of molecular properties is a critical task in drug discovery and materials science. Traditional machine learning methods often require extensive feature engineering, which can be time-consuming and may not capture the complex relationships between molecular structure and properties. In this paper, we propose the Molecular Transformer, a novel model for accurate and calibrated molecular property prediction. The Molecular Transformer uses a self-attention mechanism to capture the complex interactions between atoms in a molecule, and outputs calibrated uncertainty estimates for its predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Molecular Transformer on various molecular property prediction benchmarks, including the QM9, ESOL, and FreeSolv datasets, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

title: Directional Message Passing for Molecular Graphs
abstract: Molecular property prediction is a fundamental task in chemistry and drug discovery. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a promising approach for molecular property prediction, as they can operate directly on molecular graphs and learn representations of atoms and bonds. However, existing GNN methods for molecular property prediction often treat messages as scalar quantities, which limits their ability to capture directional information. In this paper, we propose DimeNet, a novel directional message passing network for molecular graphs. DimeNet uses directional message passing to capture the spatial relationships between atoms, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on a number of benchmark datasets for molecular property prediction, including the QM9, MD17, and OC20 datasets.

title: SchNet: A Continuous-filter Convolutional Neural Network for Modeling Quantum Interactions
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Deep learning has the potential to revolutionize quantum chemistry as it is ideally suited to learn representations for structured data and speed up the exploration of chemical space. While convolutional neural networks have gained recognition for modeling translationally invariant data in computer vision, they have not yet been successfully applied to the estimation of quantum mechanical observables. In this work, we present a deep learning architecture for the prediction of molecular properties that is based on continuous-filter convolutional layers. We demonstrate that our SchNet model accurately predicts various molecular properties across a broad range of datasets, including energies and forces for molecules in equilibrium and non-equilibrium states. SchNet achieves chemical accuracy on the QM9 benchmark dataset and is able to model the dynamics of molecular systems with high precision.

title: GNN-FiLM: Graph Neural Networks with Feature-wise Linear Modulation
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful class of models for learning representations of graph-structured data. However, existing GNN architectures often struggle to capture complex relationships between nodes, especially when the graph contains diverse edge types or when the importance of different features varies across the graph. In this paper, we propose GNN-FiLM, a novel GNN architecture that uses Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) to adaptively control the information flow in GNNs. GNN-FiLM uses a FiLM generator to produce feature-wise affine transformations that are applied to the node features at each layer, allowing the model to adaptively weight different features based on the graph structure and the task at hand. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GNN-FiLM on various graph benchmarks, including node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing GNN methods.

title: GraphNorm: A Principled Approach to Accelerating Graph Neural Network Training
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Normalization techniques have been widely used in deep learning to accelerate training and improve the performance of neural networks. However, existing normalization methods are designed for grid-like data (e.g., images) and are not directly applicable to graph-structured data. In this paper, we propose GraphNorm, a principled normalization approach specifically designed for graph neural networks (GNNs). GraphNorm addresses the unique challenges of normalizing graph data, such as the irregular structure and the varying degrees of nodes. We provide theoretical analysis showing that GraphNorm can effectively accelerate the convergence of GNN training, and demonstrate its effectiveness on various graph benchmarks. Our experimental results show that GraphNorm consistently improves the training speed and performance of GNNs across a wide range of tasks and architectures.

title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret. In this paper, we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for generating interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that are crucial for GNN's prediction, and generates explanations that are easy to understand. GNNExplainer can explain predictions for node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks, and can be applied to any GNN architecture. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GNNExplainer on various benchmarks and show that it provides more accurate and interpretable explanations than existing methods.

title: PGExplainer: Parameterized Explainer for Graph Neural Network
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in various graph-based machine learning tasks. However, understanding why GNNs make certain predictions remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose PGExplainer, a novel parameterized explainer for GNNs. Unlike existing explanation methods that are specific to individual predictions, PGExplainer learns a general explanation model that can be applied to multiple predictions. PGExplainer uses a graph neural network to parameterize the explanation generation process, and is trained to maximize the mutual information between the explanation and the GNN's predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGExplainer on various benchmarks and show that it provides more accurate and stable explanations than existing methods.

title: KG-BERT: BERT for Knowledge Graph Completion
abstract: Knowledge graph completion is the task of predicting missing links in a knowledge graph, which is important for various applications such as question answering and information retrieval. Existing methods for knowledge graph completion typically learn embeddings of entities and relations, but they may not capture the rich semantic information in the knowledge graph. In this paper, we propose KG-BERT, a novel method for knowledge graph completion that leverages the pre-trained language model BERT. KG-BERT treats triples in the knowledge graph as textual sequences and uses BERT to encode them, allowing it to capture the semantic information of entities and relations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of KG-BERT on various knowledge graph completion benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Embedding Entities and Relations for Learning and Inference in Knowledge Bases
abstract: Knowledge bases are a key component of many AI systems, but they often suffer from incompleteness. Learning embeddings of entities and relations in knowledge bases is a promising approach for predicting missing links and completing knowledge bases. In this paper, we propose DistMult, a simple and effective method for learning embeddings of entities and relations. DistMult uses a bilinear diagonal model to score triples, which allows it to efficiently capture the interactions between entities and relations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DistMult on various knowledge base completion benchmarks and show that it achieves competitive performance compared to more complex methods.

title: Graph Neural Diffusion
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, existing GNN methods often suffer from over-smoothing and over-squashing problems, which limit their ability to capture long-range dependencies in graphs. In this paper, we propose Graph Neural Diffusion (GRAND), a novel GNN framework based on graph diffusion. GRAND uses a continuous diffusion process to propagate information on the graph, which naturally alleviates the over-smoothing and over-squashing problems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GRAND on various graph benchmarks, including node classification and graph classification tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing GNN methods.

title: Expander Graph Propagation
abstract: Message passing neural networks (MPNNs) have emerged as the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning. However, MPNNs suffer from well-known limitations such as over-smoothing and over-squashing, which limit their ability to capture long-range dependencies in graphs. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Expander Graph Propagation (EGP) that addresses these limitations. EGP works by rewiring the input graph to add virtual edges that connect distant nodes, effectively reducing the graph diameter and improving information propagation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EGP on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: DiGraph: Transformer over Directed Graphs with Positional Encoding
venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
abstract: Directed graphs are a common type of graph structure in real-world applications, such as citation networks, social networks, and knowledge graphs. However, many existing graph neural network methods are designed for undirected graphs and may not effectively capture the directional information in directed graphs. In this paper, we propose DiGraph, a novel transformer architecture for directed graphs. DiGraph introduces a directional positional encoding that captures the hierarchical structure of directed graphs, and uses a transformer architecture to learn representations of nodes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DiGraph on various directed graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Do Transformers Really Perform Bad for Graph Representation?
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: The Transformer architecture has achieved great success in natural language processing and computer vision, but its application to graph representation learning remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Graphormer, a novel Transformer-based model for graph representation learning. Graphormer introduces several key design elements that are tailored for graph-structured data, including a centrality encoding that captures the importance of nodes, a spatial encoding that captures the structural relationships between nodes, and an edge encoding that captures the edge features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Graphormer on the OGB Large-Scale Challenge (OGB-LSC) and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on the graph-level prediction task, outperforming existing GNN methods by a significant margin.

title: Recipe for a General, Powerful, Scalable Graph Transformer
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Graph Transformers (GTs) have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for graph representation learning. However, existing GT methods often suffer from scalability issues and may not generalize well to different types of graphs. In this paper, we propose GraphGPS, a general, powerful, and scalable graph transformer. GraphGPS combines the strengths of message passing neural networks and transformers, using a novel hybrid architecture that can capture both local and global graph structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GraphGPS on a wide range of graph benchmarks, including molecular property prediction, node classification, and graph classification tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being scalable to large graphs.

title: Structure-Aware Transformer for Graph Representation Learning
abstract: Transformers have shown great promise for graph representation learning, but they often struggle to capture the structural information of graphs. In this paper, we propose the Structure-Aware Transformer (SAT), a novel transformer architecture that explicitly incorporates structural information into the attention mechanism. SAT uses a structural encoding that captures the relative positions of nodes in the graph, and uses this encoding to modulate the attention scores. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SAT on various graph benchmarks, including graph classification and node classification tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing transformer and GNN methods.

title: Training Graph Neural Networks with 1000 Layers
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in various graph-based machine learning tasks. However, training very deep GNNs remains a challenging task due to the vanishing gradient problem and the over-smoothing issue. In this paper, we propose RevGNN, a reversible graph neural network that enables training GNNs with up to 1000 layers. RevGNN uses a reversible architecture that allows the activations to be recomputed during backpropagation, significantly reducing the memory consumption. We also propose a group convolution strategy that reduces the computational cost of training deep GNNs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RevGNN on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance with very deep architectures.

title: Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation for Graph Nets
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been shown to be effective for learning representations of graph-structured data. However, existing GNN methods often use a single aggregation operation, such as sum, mean, or max, which may not capture the full complexity of the graph structure. In this paper, we propose Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA), a novel aggregation method for GNNs. PNA combines multiple aggregation operations (sum, mean, max, min, std) with degree-based scalers, allowing it to capture a wide range of graph structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PNA on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on both graph-level and node-level tasks.

title: Directional Graph Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are often limited in their ability to capture directional information in graphs, as they typically treat all neighbors equally. In this paper, we propose Directional Graph Networks (DGNs), a novel GNN architecture that captures directional information by defining anisotropic aggregation operations. DGN uses the gradient of the low-frequency eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian to define directions on the graph, and uses these directions to guide the message passing process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DGN on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on both graph-level and node-level tasks.

title: Improving Graph Neural Network Expressivity via Subgraph Isomorphism Counting
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in learning representations for graph-structured data, they are known to have limited expressive power, often no more powerful than the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test. In this paper, we propose Graph Substructure Networks (GSNs), a novel GNN architecture that enhances the expressive power of GNNs by incorporating subgraph isomorphism counting. GSN counts the occurrences of small subgraphs (motifs) in the neighborhood of each node and uses these counts as additional features for the GNN. We demonstrate that GSN is strictly more expressive than the WL test and achieves state-of-the-art performance on various graph classification benchmarks.

title: A Theory of Using Graph Neural Networks for Multi-Node Representation Learning
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful models for learning representations of nodes in graphs. However, existing GNN methods are primarily designed for single-node representation learning, and their theoretical understanding for multi-node representation learning is limited. In this paper, we present a theoretical framework for using GNNs for multi-node representation learning, which is important for tasks such as link prediction and subgraph classification. We show that GNNs can be viewed as kernel methods and analyze their expressive power for multi-node representation learning. Based on our theoretical analysis, we propose GNN-AK, a novel GNN architecture that enhances the expressive power of GNNs for multi-node representation learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GNN-AK on various benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: LinkX: A Unified Framework for Link Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph machine learning, with applications in social network analysis, recommendation systems, and knowledge graph completion. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for link prediction, but existing methods often focus on specific types of graphs or link prediction scenarios. In this paper, we propose LinkX, a unified framework for link prediction with GNNs. LinkX is designed to handle various types of graphs and link prediction scenarios, including homogeneous graphs, heterogeneous graphs, and temporal graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LinkX on various link prediction benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance across different graph types.

title: Graph Neural Networks with Local Features
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, existing GNN methods often rely on global feature transformations, which may not capture the local structure of the graph effectively. In this paper, we propose GNN-LF, a novel GNN architecture that uses local features to enhance the representational power of GNNs. GNN-LF extracts local features from the neighborhood of each node and uses these features to guide the message passing process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GNN-LF on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on both node-level and graph-level tasks.

title: MixHop: Higher-Order Graph Convolutional Architectures via Sparsified Neighborhood Mixing
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and their variants have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, existing GCN methods typically only aggregate information from the immediate neighbors of each node, which limits their ability to capture higher-order structural information. In this paper, we propose MixHop, a higher-order graph convolutional architecture that aggregates information from a mix of different neighborhood ranges. MixHop uses a sparsified neighborhood mixing strategy to efficiently capture higher-order information without significantly increasing the computational cost. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MixHop on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on node classification and link prediction tasks.

title: Geom-GCN: Geometric Graph Convolutional Networks
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, existing GCN methods are primarily designed for homophilic graphs, where connected nodes tend to have similar features or labels. In this paper, we propose Geom-GCN, a novel geometric graph convolutional network that is effective for both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. Geom-GCN uses a geometric aggregation scheme that captures the structural information of the graph, and a bi-level aggregation mechanism that aggregates information from both the structural neighborhood and the feature neighborhood. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Geom-GCN on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on heterophilic graphs.

title: Beyond Low-Pass Filters: Adaptive Feature Propagation on Graphs
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a popular class of graph neural networks that use low-pass filters to smooth node features. While low-pass filters are effective for homophilic graphs, they may not be suitable for heterophilic graphs where connected nodes have dissimilar features. In this paper, we propose a novel adaptive feature propagation framework that goes beyond low-pass filters. Our framework uses both low-pass and high-pass filters to adaptively propagate features on graphs, allowing it to handle both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on heterophilic graphs.

title: Graph World Models
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, existing GNN methods often focus on static graphs and may not effectively capture the temporal dynamics of evolving graphs. In this paper, we propose Graph World Models (GWMs), a novel framework for learning representations of dynamic graphs. GWMs use a world model to predict the future state of the graph, and use these predictions to learn better representations of the current state. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GWMs on various dynamic graph benchmarks and show that they achieve state-of-the-art performance on link prediction and node classification tasks.

title: GRAND: Graph Neural Diffusion
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, existing GNN methods often suffer from over-smoothing and over-squashing problems, which limit their ability to capture long-range dependencies in graphs. In this paper, we propose GRAND, a novel graph neural diffusion model that addresses these limitations. GRAND uses a continuous diffusion process to propagate information on the graph, which naturally alleviates the over-smoothing and over-squashing problems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GRAND on various graph benchmarks, including node classification and graph classification tasks, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing GNN methods.

title: Graph State Space Models
abstract: State space models (SSMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to transformers for sequential data, offering linear computational complexity and the ability to capture long-range dependencies. In this paper, we propose Graph State Space Models (S4G), a novel architecture that extends state space models to graph-structured data. S4G uses a state space formulation to model the propagation of information on graphs, allowing it to capture long-range dependencies with linear complexity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of S4G on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves competitive performance compared to existing GNN and transformer methods while being significantly more efficient.

title: Scene Graph Generation by Iterative Message Passing
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
abstract: Scene graph generation is the task of generating a structured representation of an image, where nodes represent objects and edges represent the relationships between objects. This task is important for various applications in computer vision, including image understanding, visual question answering, and image captioning. In this paper, we propose a novel scene graph generation framework based on iterative message passing. Our framework uses a graph neural network to iteratively refine the object and relationship predictions, allowing it to capture the complex dependencies between objects. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on the Visual Genome dataset and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Neural Bellman-Ford Networks: A General Graph Neural Network Framework for Link Prediction
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph machine learning, with applications in social network analysis, recommendation systems, and knowledge graph completion. Existing link prediction methods often rely on heuristic features or graph neural networks (GNNs) with limited receptive fields. In this paper, we propose Neural Bellman-Ford Networks (NBForest), a general graph neural network framework for link prediction. NBForest is inspired by the Bellman-Ford algorithm and uses a generalized shortest path formulation to compute node representations. This allows NBForest to capture long-range dependencies in the graph and achieve state-of-the-art performance on various link prediction benchmarks.

title: UltraGCN: Ultra Simplification of Graph Convolutional Networks for Recommendation
venue: Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Information & Knowledge Management
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a popular choice for collaborative filtering in recommendation systems. However, the training of GCNs can be computationally expensive, especially for large-scale recommendation datasets. In this paper, we propose UltraGCN, an ultra-simplified graph convolutional network for recommendation. UltraGCN directly approximates the limit of infinite-layer graph convolutions via a constraint-based loss function, avoiding the expensive iterative message passing process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of UltraGCN on various recommendation benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being orders of magnitude faster than existing GCN-based methods.

title: Bootstrap Your Own Latent: A New Approach to Self-Supervised Learning of Graph Representations
abstract: Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations without labeled data. In this paper, we propose BGRL, a novel self-supervised learning method for graph representations. BGRL uses a bootstrap mechanism to learn representations by predicting the outputs of a target network using an online network. This approach avoids the need for negative samples, which are often difficult to generate for graph data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BGRL on various graph benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on node classification and link prediction tasks.

title: Aphynity: Augmenting Physical Models with Neural Networks
abstract: Physical models provide a principled approach for understanding and predicting the behavior of complex systems, but they often rely on simplifying assumptions that may not hold in practice. In this paper, we propose APHYNITY, a framework for augmenting physical models with neural networks. APHYNITY uses a neural network to learn the residual between the physical model's predictions and the true observations, allowing it to combine the strengths of physical modeling and data-driven learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of APHYNITY on various physical systems, including fluid dynamics and molecular dynamics, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: GNNGuard: Defending Graph Neural Networks Against Adversarial Attacks
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in various graph-based machine learning tasks. However, recent studies have shown that GNNs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations to the graph structure or node features can lead to incorrect predictions. In this paper, we propose GNNGuard, a novel defense mechanism against adversarial attacks on GNNs. GNNGuard uses a robust aggregation mechanism that down-weights the influence of potentially adversarial edges, and a graph purification mechanism that removes adversarial edges from the graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GNNGuard on various benchmarks and show that it significantly improves the robustness of GNNs against adversarial attacks.

title: Graph Neural Factorization Machines for Feature Interaction Learning
venue: Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Information & Knowledge Management
abstract: Factorization Machines (FMs) are a popular class of models for learning feature interactions in recommendation systems and click-through rate prediction. However, existing FM methods may not effectively capture the structural relationships between features. In this paper, we propose Graph Neural Factorization Machines (GNN-FMs), a novel architecture that combines the strengths of Graph Neural Networks and Factorization Machines. GNN-FMs use a graph neural network to learn representations of features and their interactions, allowing it to capture both the feature interactions and the structural relationships between features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GNN-FMs on various recommendation and click-through rate prediction benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Open Graph Benchmark: Datasets for Machine Learning on Graphs
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
abstract: We present the Open Graph Benchmark (OGB), a diverse and challenging set of benchmark datasets for machine learning on graphs. OGB includes realistic large-scale datasets from a variety of domains, including social networks, molecular graphs, and knowledge graphs. OGB also includes a unified evaluation framework that allows for fair comparison of different methods. We demonstrate the utility of OGB by evaluating a wide range of graph neural network methods on the benchmark datasets, and show that there is significant room for improvement on many of the tasks. We believe that OGB will facilitate the development of new and better methods for machine learning on graphs.

title: Graph Adversarial Networks: Protecting Information against Adversarial Attacks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations to the graph structure or node features can significantly degrade the performance of the model. In this paper, we propose FLAG, a free large-scale adversarial augmentation method for GNNs. FLAG works by adding adversarial perturbations to the node features during training, which improves the robustness of the model without requiring additional data or computational resources. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FLAG on various graph benchmarks and show that it significantly improves the robustness and generalization performance of GNNs.

title: Hierarchical Graph Network for Multi-hop Question Answering
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
abstract: Multi-hop question answering (QA) is a challenging task that requires reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence to answer complex questions. In this paper, we propose the Hierarchical Graph Network (HGN), a novel architecture for multi-hop QA. HGN constructs a hierarchical graph that captures the relationships between entities, paragraphs, and documents, and uses a graph neural network to reason over the graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HGN on various multi-hop QA benchmarks, including HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Graph4NLP: An Open-Source Library for Deep Learning on Graphs for Natural Language Processing
abstract: Graphs are a natural representation for structured data in natural language processing (NLP), including syntactic parse trees, semantic role graphs, and knowledge graphs. However, existing deep learning libraries for NLP often do not provide adequate support for graph-based methods. In this paper, we present Graph4NLP, an open-source library for deep learning on graphs for NLP. Graph4NLP provides a comprehensive set of tools for building graph-based NLP models, including graph construction, graph encoding, and graph decoding modules. We demonstrate the utility of Graph4NLP by implementing various state-of-the-art graph-based NLP models and evaluating them on multiple benchmarks.

title: Graph Neural Networks with Generated Parameters for Relation Extraction
venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
abstract: Relation extraction is a fundamental task in natural language processing that involves identifying semantic relationships between entities in text. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been shown to be effective for relation extraction, but they often require a large number of parameters to capture the diverse relationships in text. In this paper, we propose a novel GNN architecture with generated parameters for relation extraction. Our method uses a hypernetwork to generate the parameters of the GNN based on the input text, allowing it to capture the diverse relationships with fewer parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various relation extraction benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: RAT-SQL: Relation-Aware Schema Encoding and Linking for Text-to-SQL Parsers
venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
abstract: Text-to-SQL is the task of converting natural language questions into SQL queries, which is important for enabling non-experts to interact with databases. In this paper, we propose RAT-SQL, a relation-aware transformer for text-to-SQL parsing. RAT-SQL uses a relation-aware self-attention mechanism that captures the relationships between schema items and question words, and a schema linking mechanism that aligns the question with the database schema. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RAT-SQL on the Spider benchmark and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: A*Net: A Scalable Path-based Reasoning Approach for Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Knowledge graph reasoning is the task of inferring new facts from existing knowledge, which is important for various applications such as question answering and recommendation systems. Path-based reasoning methods have shown promise for knowledge graph reasoning, but they often suffer from scalability issues. In this paper, we propose A*Net, a scalable path-based reasoning approach for knowledge graphs. A*Net uses an adaptive path search algorithm that efficiently explores the knowledge graph and finds relevant paths for reasoning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of A*Net on various knowledge graph reasoning benchmarks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being significantly more efficient than existing methods.

title: ReaRev: Adaptive Reasoning for Question Answering over Knowledge Graphs
venue: Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
abstract: Question answering over knowledge graphs (KGQA) is a challenging task that requires reasoning over the structured knowledge in a knowledge graph to answer natural language questions. In this paper, we propose ReaRev, an adaptive reasoning approach for KGQA. ReaRev uses a reinforcement learning-based approach to adaptively select the reasoning path over the knowledge graph, allowing it to efficiently find the answer to the question. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ReaRev on various KGQA benchmarks, including MetaQA and WebQuestionsSP, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

title: Are Multimodal LLMs Ready for Clinical Dermatology? A Real-World Evaluation in Dermatology
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promise on publicly available dermatology benchmarks. However, benchmark performance may not generalize to real-world dermatologic decision-making. To quantify this benchmark-to-bedside gap, we evaluated four open-weight MLLMs (InternVL-Chat v1.5, LLaVA-Med v1.5, SkinGPT4 and MedGemma-4B-Instruct) and one commercial MLLM (GPT-4.1) across three publicly available dermatology datasets and a retrospective multi-site hospital-based dermatology consultation cohort comprising 5,811 cases and 46,405 clinical images. Models were evaluated on two clinically relevant tasks: differential diagnosis generation and severity-based triage. Diagnostic performance was modest on public datasets and declined substantially in the real-world cohort. On public benchmarks, top-3 diagnostic accuracy reached 26.55% for the best open-weight model and 42.25% for GPT-4.1. On real-world consultation cases using images alone, top-3 diagnostic accuracy fell to 1.50%-13.35% among open-weight models and 24.65% for GPT-4.1. Incorporating clinical context improved performance across all models, increasing top-3 diagnostic accuracy up to 28.75% among open-weight models and 38.93% for GPT-4.1. However, model outputs were highly sensitive to incomplete or erroneous consultation context. For severity-based triage, models achieved moderate sensitivity (above 60%), suggesting potential utility for screening but insufficient reliability for clinical deployment. These findings demonstrate that benchmark performance substantially overestimates the real-world clinical capability of current dermatology MLLMs.

title: A Novel Multimodal RUL Framework for Remaining Useful Life Estimation with Layer-wise Explanations
abstract: Estimating the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of mechanical systems is pivotal in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). Rolling-element bearings are among the most frequent causes of machinery failure, highlighting the need for robust RUL estimation methods. Existing approaches often suffer from poor generalization, lack of robustness, high data demands, and limited interpretability. This paper proposes a novel multimodal-RUL framework that jointly leverages image representations (ImR) and time-frequency representations (TFR) of multichannel, nonstationary vibration signals. The architecture comprises three branches: (1) an ImR branch and (2) a TFR branch, both employing multiple dilated convolutional blocks with residual connections to extract spatial degradation features; and (3) a fusion branch that concatenates these features and feeds them into an LSTM to model temporal degradation patterns. A multi-head attention mechanism subsequently emphasizes salient features, followed by linear layers for final RUL regression. To enable effective multimodal learning, vibration signals are converted into ImR via the Bresenham line algorithm and into TFR using Continuous Wavelet Transform. We also introduce multimodal Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (multimodal-LRP), a tailored explainability technique that significantly enhances model transparency. The approach is validated on the XJTU-SY and PRONOSTIA benchmark datasets. Results show that our method matches or surpasses state-of-the-art baselines under both seen and unseen operating conditions, while requiring ~28 % less training data on XJTU-SY and ~48 % less on PRONOSTIA. The model exhibits strong noise resilience, and multimodal-LRP visualizations confirm the interpretability and trustworthiness of predictions, making the framework highly suitable for real-world industrial deployment.

title: CheXmix: Unified Generative Pretraining for Vision Language Models in Medical Imaging
abstract: Recent medical multimodal foundation models are built as multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) by connecting a CLIP-pretrained vision encoder to an LLM using LLaVA-style finetuning. This two-stage, decoupled approach introduces a projection layer that can distort visual features. This is especially concerning in medical imaging where subtle cues are essential for accurate diagnoses. In contrast, early-fusion generative approaches such as Chameleon eliminate the projection bottleneck by processing image and text tokens within a single unified sequence, enabling joint representation learning that leverages the inductive priors of language models. We present CheXmix, a unified early-fusion generative model trained on a large corpus of chest X-rays paired with radiology reports. We expand on Chameleon's autoregressive framework by introducing a two-stage multimodal generative pretraining strategy that combines the representational strengths of masked autoencoders with MLLMs. The resulting models are highly flexible, supporting both discriminative and generative tasks at both coarse and fine-grained scales. Our approach outperforms well-established generative models across all masking ratios by 6.0% and surpasses CheXagent by 8.6% on AUROC at high image masking ratios on the CheXpert classification task. We further inpaint images over 51.0% better than text-only generative models and outperform CheXagent by 45% on the GREEN metric for radiology report generation. These results demonstrate that CheXmix captures fine-grained information across a broad spectrum of chest X-ray tasks. Our code is at: https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/CheXmix.

title: Do We Really Need External Tools to Mitigate Hallucinations? SIRA: Shared-Prefix Internal Reconstruction of Attribution
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate when language priors dominate weak or ambiguous visual evidence. Existing contrastive decoding methods mitigate this problem by comparing predictions from the original image with those from externally perturbed visual inputs, but such references can introduce off-manifold artifacts and require costly extra forward passes. We propose SIRA, a training-free internal contrastive decoding framework that constructs a counterfactual reference inside the same LVLM by exploiting the staged information flow of multimodal transformers. Instead of removing visual information from the input, SIRA first lets image and text tokens interact through a shared prefix, forming an aligned multimodal state that preserves prompt interpretation, decoding history, positional structure, and early visual grounding. It then forks a counterfactual branch in later transformer layers, where attention to image-token positions is masked. This branch retains the shared multimodal context but lacks continued access to fine-grained visual evidence, yielding a language-prior-dominated internal reference for token-level contrast. During decoding, SIRA suppresses tokens that remain strong without late visual access and favors predictions whose advantage depends on the full visual pathway. Experiments on POPE, CHAIR, and AMBER with Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA-v1.5 show that SIRA consistently reduces hallucinations while preserving descriptive coverage and incurring lower overhead than two-pass contrastive decoding. SIRA requires no training, external verifier, or perturbed input, and applies to open-weight LVLMs with white-box inference access.

title: Conceptualizing Embeddings: Sparse Disentanglement for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models learn powerful multimodal embeddings, yet their internal semantics remain opaque. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable features, they rely on expanding the representation dimension, which compromises the original geometry and introduces redundancy. We introduce CEDAR (Conceptual Embedding Disentanglement via Adaptive Rotation), a post-hoc method that reveals the compositional structure of pretrained embeddings without increasing dimensionality. By learning an invertible transformation with a top-$k$ sparsity bottleneck, CEDAR concentrates semantic information into axis-aligned disentangled coordinates. In CLIP-like architecture, individual coordinates can be interpreted with textual concepts, while for generative models such as BLIP, they can be decoded into natural language descriptions. Experiments demonstrate that CEDAR achieves a competitive reconstruction-sparsity trade-off while producing explanations that are more interpretable and better aligned with human perception. Our results suggest that the apparent entanglement in vision-language representations can be resolved through a suitable change of basis, eliminating the need for overcomplete expansions.

title: PGT: Procedurally Generated Tasks for improving visual grounding in MLLMs
abstract: Despite remarkable progress in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), these models still struggle with fine-grained understanding tasks. In this work, we propose Procedurally Generated Tasks (PGT), a simple data-driven framework that serves a dual purpose: inducing fine-grained visual understanding and acting as a low-cost diagnostic tool to identify the source of perception failures. By overlaying unambiguous geometric primitives on images, PGT generate additional dense supervision that disentangles visual grounding capability from semantic priors. Extensive experiments on relational, quantitative, and 3D/depth understanding benchmarks show that PGT yields remarkable gains across diverse architectures. Instruction tuning MLLMs on LLaVA-v1.5-Instruct augmented with PGT data results in improvements of up to +20% on the What'sUp benchmark and +13.3% on CV-Bench-2D, while maintaining general perception capabilities. Moreover, finetuning state-of-the-art MLLMs on PGT data leads to boosts of up to +5.5% on What'sUp and +8.3% on CV-Bench-2D. These findings demonstrate that PGT effectively address the bottleneck of fine-grained perception, revealing that many spatial reasoning deficits stem from inadequate supervision signals rather than inherent architectural or resolution limitations.

title: Video Active Perception: Effective Inference-Time Long-Form Video Understanding with Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced multimodal tasks such as video question answering (QA). However, VLMs face the challenge of selecting frames effectively and efficiently, as standard uniform sampling is expensive and performance may plateau. Inspired by active perception theory, which posits that models gain information by acquiring data that differs from their expectations, we introduce Video Active Perception (VAP), a training-free method to enhance long-form video QA using VLMs. Our approach treats keyframe selection as data acquisition in active perception and leverages a lightweight text-conditioned video generation model to represent prior world knowledge. Empirically, VAP achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results on long-form or reasoning video QA datasets such as EgoSchema, NExT-QA, ActivityNet-QA, IntentQA, and CLEVRER, achieving an increase of up to 5.6 x frame efficiency by frames per question over standard GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LLaVA-OV. Moreover, VAP shows stronger reasoning abilities than previous methods and effectively selects keyframes relevant to questions. These findings highlight the potential of leveraging active perception to improve the frame effectiveness and efficiency of long-form video QA.

title: A Deep Learning Approach to Interface Color Quality Assessment in HCI
abstract: In this paper, a quantitative evaluation model for the color quality of human-computer interaction interfaces is proposed by combining deep convolutional neural networks (CNN). By extracting multidimensional features of interface images, including hue, brightness, purity, etc., CNN is used for efficient feature modeling and quantitative analysis, and the relationship between interface design and user perception is studied. The experiment is based on multiple international mainstream website interface datasets, covering e-commerce platforms, social media, education platforms, etc., and verifies the evaluation effect of the model on indicators such as contrast, clarity, color coordination, and visual appeal. The results show that the CNN evaluation is highly consistent with the user rating, with a correlation coefficient of up to 0.96, and it also shows high accuracy in mean square error and absolute error. Compared with traditional experience-based evaluation methods, the proposed model can efficiently and scientifically capture the visual characteristics of the interface and avoid the influence of subjective factors. Future research can explore the introduction of multimodal data (such as text and interactive behavior) into the model to further enhance the evaluation ability of dynamic interfaces and expand it to fields such as smart homes, medical systems, and virtual reality. This paper provides new methods and new ideas for the scientific evaluation and optimization of interface design.

title: Zero-Shot Recognition of Dysarthric Speech Using Commercial Automatic Speech Recognition and Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Voice-based human-machine interaction is a primary modality for accessing intelligent systems, yet individuals with dysarthria face systematic exclusion due to recognition performance gaps. Whilst automatic speech recognition (ASR) achieves word error rates (WER) below 5% on typical speech, performance degrades dramatically for dysarthric speakers.
